nodes.l1: A hard lump of rock. Heavy, dull, and one of the most consequential objects in this entire graph.
nodes.l2: Rock is not a technology. It becomes one the moment somebody notices that it breaks in predictable ways. Certain stones — flint, chert, obsidian, quartzite — fracture along smooth curved surfaces when struck at the right angle, which means their edges can be controlled rather than merely found. Almost every tool tradition of the next three million years begins with someone reading that property correctly.
nodes.l3: Stone is the reason we can see deep prehistory at all. Wood, hide, fibre and skin rot; knapped stone does not. The entire early archaeological record is biased toward whatever survives, which is mostly rock and bone — a distortion researchers call preservation bias, and one worth remembering before concluding that early people 'only' had stone.
nodes.ev: Geology and archaeological site material

nodes.l1: Strong along the grain, easy to shape, and almost invisible in the archaeological record.
nodes.l2: Wood is the material early technology was probably mostly made of, and the one we have almost no evidence for. It carries load, holds an edge poorly but a point well, floats, and burns. Handles, hafts, shafts, frames, containers, traps and boats are all wood problems before they are anything else.
nodes.l3: Waterlogged and anaerobic sites preserve wood when normal ground does not. The Schöningen spears from Germany — worked wooden throwing spears roughly 300,000 years old — survived because they sat in wet lake sediment. Finds like these show that the wooden component of early toolkits was sophisticated, and that its usual absence is about preservation, not ability.
nodes.ev: Waterlogged-site finds; Schöningen spears
nodes.caution: Absence of wooden artefacts is evidence of decay, not of simplicity.

nodes.l1: A material that arrives as a by-product of eating and turns out to be excellent for making things.
nodes.l2: Bone, antler and ivory are tougher and less brittle than stone. They take a fine point without shattering, which is exactly what stone cannot do. Bone also stores marrow — a dense fat source that is only accessible if you can break the shaft open, which requires a tool and a technique.
nodes.l3: Cut marks and percussion damage on animal bone are among the clearest early signals of tool use, because a stone edge leaves a V-shaped groove that a carnivore tooth does not. Zooarchaeologists distinguish the two under magnification, and the pattern of marks reveals butchery order, not just presence.
nodes.ev: Cut-marked faunal remains; worked bone tools

nodes.l1: Bark, sinew, gut, vine, hair. Individually weak. Twisted together, transformative.
nodes.l2: A single plant fibre snaps under almost no load. Several fibres twisted in opposition lock against each other by friction and become a cord that can hold a person's weight. This is the first structural material humans manufactured rather than collected, and it is the precondition for hafting, nets, traps, bows, sails and sewn clothing.
nodes.l3: Fibre survives even less often than wood. A twisted three-ply cord fragment found on a Neanderthal-associated stone flake at Abri du Maras, France, is one of the very few direct traces, and it is only a few centimetres long. Most of the evidence is indirect: impressions in clay, wear patterns on tools, and objects that could not function without cordage.
nodes.ev: Rare direct cord fragments; impressions; use-wear
nodes.caution: Direct fibre evidence is extremely rare; most inferences come from indirect traces.

nodes.l1: A rock with an edge. Not yet designed — but no longer just a rock.
nodes.l2: The gap between a naturally broken stone and a deliberately broken one is the whole beginning of technology. A sharp edge lets a soft-handed, blunt-toothed primate cut through hide it could not otherwise open. That single capability changes what counts as food.
nodes.l3: Lomekwi 3 in Kenya has produced very early flaked stone dated to roughly 3.3 million years ago, older than the genus Homo. Interpretation is debated — distinguishing intentional flaking from natural fracture is genuinely hard, and researchers argue about it in print, which is how the question should be settled.
nodes.ev: Early flaked stone assemblages
nodes.caution: The earliest claimed stone tools are contested; natural fracture can mimic deliberate flaking.

nodes.l1: The piece that comes off — and often the piece you actually wanted.
nodes.l2: Knapping produces two things: a core and the flakes struck from it. For a long time archaeologists assumed the core was the tool. Increasingly the flakes look like the point of the exercise: thin, extremely sharp, disposable, and producible in quantity from one good cobble. A working edge you can make ten of is a different kind of technology from one you have to preserve.
nodes.l3: Refitting studies — physically reassembling scattered flakes back onto their core like a three-dimensional jigsaw — reconstruct the exact sequence of blows. They show planning, error correction, and in some cases a knapper stopping and restarting, which is about as close to watching the process as archaeology gets.
nodes.ev: Refitted lithic assemblages; Oldowan industry

nodes.l1: A shaped object made to do a job. The first thing in this graph that was designed.
nodes.l2: A shaped tool implies something a flake does not: a mental template held before the work begins, and maintained across dozens of blows. The Acheulean handaxe holds roughly the same symmetrical form across a million years and three continents — a persistence that says the design was being taught, not reinvented.
nodes.l3: Experimental archaeology tests this directly. Modern knappers learn to reproduce the forms, and researchers measure how long the skill takes to acquire and whether it can be learned by imitation alone. The results feed a live debate about when teaching — as opposed to copying — became part of how humans transmit skill.
nodes.ev: Acheulean assemblages; experimental replication
nodes.caution: 'Tool use' is not unique to humans; chimpanzees, crows and otters use tools. Deliberate shaping to a repeated template is the sharper distinction.

nodes.l1: Separating material along a line. Boring, until you consider what it unlocks.
nodes.l2: Human teeth and nails cannot open a large carcass. A stone edge can. Cutting converts a dead animal from an inaccessible object into food, hide, sinew and bone — four materials at once. It also makes fibre processing possible, which is the doorway to cordage.
nodes.l3: Microwear analysis reads the polish and striations left on a tool's edge under high magnification, and different worked materials leave different signatures — hide, wood, bone and plant each polish stone differently. This lets researchers say what a tool cut, not merely that it was used.
nodes.ev: Microwear and residue analysis

nodes.l1: Removing material from a surface without cutting through it.
nodes.l2: Scraping is what makes a hide into leather and a branch into a shaft. It is slow, repetitive work, and the tools show it: scrapers are among the most resharpened and longest-curated objects in early assemblages. Someone was carrying these around rather than making a new one each time.
nodes.l3: Edge angle is the tell. Cutting edges are acute; scraping edges are steep, typically 60–90 degrees, because a steep edge removes material without digging in. Assemblages can be sorted by function on this basis before any wear analysis is done.
nodes.ev: Edge-angle analysis; curated scraper assemblages

nodes.l1: Applying force through a hard object. The oldest way to make something happen.
nodes.l2: Percussion does two jobs. It makes other tools, since knapping is controlled hammering. And it opens things that resist opening — nuts, bone shafts, shellfish. Marrow and brain are dense fat and calorie sources available to nobody who cannot break bone.
nodes.l3: Hammerstones are identifiable by battering damage on their ends, and pitted anvil stones show the reciprocal wear. At some sites the two are found together with broken nutshell, which lets researchers reconstruct a specific processing station rather than a general activity.
nodes.ev: Battered hammerstones; anvil stones; percussion marks

nodes.l1: Two or more materials joined so that each does what the other cannot.
nodes.l2: A stone point is sharp but cannot be thrown far. A wooden shaft carries distance but has no edge. Joined, they are a weapon that works at a range where the animal cannot reach you. Hafting also multiplies the force delivered to a small edge, which is why a hafted axe cuts wood that a hand-held flake cannot.
nodes.l3: Adhesive residues survive better than the bindings themselves. Birch-bark tar on Middle Palaeolithic stone points is direct evidence of hafting — and producing that tar requires heating bark under controlled, low-oxygen conditions, which is a multi-step chemical process in its own right.
nodes.ev: Adhesive residues; impact fractures on points

nodes.l1: Fibres twisted against each other until friction makes them strong.
nodes.l2: Cordage is an invisible keystone. Nets, snares, bows, fishing lines, sewn clothing, hafted tools, rafts and carrying bags all require it, and none of them survive without it. When you find any of those, you have found cordage by implication.
nodes.l3: The Abri du Maras cord fragment — three bundles of fibre twisted counter to the ply direction — is a rare direct find. The counter-twist matters: it is the mechanical principle that stops the cord unravelling, and it is not obvious. Somebody worked it out.
nodes.ev: Rare cord fragments; tool impressions

nodes.l1: Holding two things together permanently enough to hit something with them.
nodes.l2: Lashing solves a mechanical problem that looks trivial and is not: a joint must resist forces from several directions at once while absorbing shock. Get it wrong and the point flies off on the first strike. Most binding traditions combine cord with adhesive because neither alone survives impact.
nodes.l3: Impact fractures on stone points show they were used as projectiles. When those points also carry adhesive traces, the inference to a bound, hafted weapon is direct rather than assumed.
nodes.ev: Adhesive traces; impact fracture patterns

nodes.l1: Joining flexible sheets with a thread that passes through them.
nodes.l2: Draped hide keeps out some cold. Sewn, fitted clothing keeps out much more, because it traps a still layer of air against the body and closes the gaps at neck, wrist and ankle. This is the difference between surviving a cold night and surviving a cold latitude year-round.
nodes.l3: Eyed needles are the diagnostic artefact — a needle without an eye is an awl, and awls only pierce. The appearance of eyed needles in the archaeological record is used as a proxy for tailored clothing, and it correlates with expansion into colder environments.
nodes.ev: Eyed bone needles; awls

nodes.l1: A thin shaft with a hole drilled through one end. Deceptively difficult to make.
nodes.l2: Making a needle means grinding bone to a fine taper without snapping it, then drilling an eye through a shaft only a couple of millimetres across. The failure rate is high and the finished object is fragile. People made them anyway, which tells you what tailored clothing was worth.
nodes.l3: Broken needle blanks are as informative as finished ones — they show the production sequence and where it usually failed. Some sites yield far more blanks than complete needles, which is the signature of a difficult craft being practised.
nodes.ev: Finished needles and failed blanks

nodes.l1: A portable microclimate worn on the body.
nodes.l2: Clothing is thermal engineering. It decouples where a hairless tropical primate can live from where its physiology allows, and that decoupling is what puts humans in Siberia, on high plateaus and eventually across an ice-age land bridge. It is also, almost immediately, a social signal.
nodes.l3: One of the more inventive proxies is genetic: clothing lice diverged from head lice at some point, and that divergence can only happen once there are clothes to live in. Molecular dating of the split gives a rough window, though the error bars are wide and the method is debated.
nodes.ev: Eyed needles; hide-working tools; clothing-louse divergence
nodes.caution: Dates for the origin of clothing rest largely on indirect proxies and remain uncertain.

nodes.l1: A constructed space that is warmer, drier and safer than outside it.
nodes.l2: A built shelter is different in kind from an occupied cave. It can be placed where the resources are rather than where the geology allows, which means the landscape stops dictating the settlement pattern. It also creates the first interior — a bounded space with an inside and an outside, which turns out to matter socially as much as thermally.
nodes.l3: Structures are read from their traces rather than their walls: post-holes, stone rings weighing down a cover, concentrations of debris that stop abruptly at a line. Mammoth-bone structures on the Russian plain survive because the frame itself was mineral.
nodes.ev: Post-holes; stone circles; mammoth-bone structures

nodes.l1: A point held at the far end of a shaft. Reach as a weapon.
nodes.l2: The spear changes the geometry of hunting. Distance means the hunter can act before the animal can, and a thrown spear extends that further. Everything about human hunting — cooperation, planning, tracking — is built on top of a tool that buys separation.
nodes.l3: The Schöningen spears are the strongest evidence: worked wooden throwing spears roughly two metres long, weighted forward like a modern javelin, from a site with butchered horse remains. They are around 300,000 years old and they were engineered, not merely sharpened.
nodes.ev: Schöningen wooden spears; impact-fractured points

nodes.date: Debated; clear evidence by ≈ 400,000 years ago
nodes.l1: Coordinated pursuit of animals that do not wish to be caught.
nodes.l2: Hunting is less a technology than an organisational problem. It requires shared intention across several people, a plan that survives contact with a moving animal, and a division of the result afterwards that everyone accepts. The weapons are the easy part.
nodes.l3: Distinguishing hunting from scavenging is a real methodological fight. The evidence is in the details: whether stone cut marks lie above or beneath carnivore tooth marks, and whether the prey are prime adults — which scavengers rarely get — or the old and sick.
nodes.ev: Cut-mark stratigraphy; prey age profiles
nodes.caution: Early hominin meat-eating may have been largely scavenging; the hunting/scavenging balance is actively debated.

nodes.l1: Taking food from water, where you cannot see or reach it.
nodes.l2: Fish are a dense, renewable protein source that most predators on land cannot access. Exploiting them requires tools that work at a distance through an opaque medium — hooks, lines, nets, traps, weirs — and it rewards settling near water rather than following herds.
nodes.l3: Fish bone is small and fragile, so it is missed unless excavators wet-sieve through fine mesh. Where sieving is done, fish frequently turn out to be a much larger part of the diet than the hand-collected assemblage suggested. Stable isotope analysis of human bone gives an independent check.
nodes.ev: Sieved fish remains; shell hooks; isotope signatures

nodes.l1: A chemical reaction that releases stored energy as heat and light.
nodes.l2: Fire is the first external energy source humans directed. Everything downstream that involves changing a material by heating it — cooking, pottery, smelting, glass, steam, engines — is a descendant of somebody learning to keep a flame alive on purpose.
nodes.l3: Proving control rather than opportunism is the hard part, since lightning also makes fire. The evidence archaeologists look for is repetition and containment: the same spot burned many times, heat-altered sediment, ash lenses with structure, burnt bone in a bounded area.
nodes.ev: Burnt sediment; ash lenses; heat-altered artefacts
nodes.caution: The date of first controlled fire is genuinely contested; claims range across hundreds of thousands of years and depend on how 'control' is defined.

nodes.l1: Fire kept in one place, at a chosen intensity, for as long as you want it.
nodes.l2: Control is the whole thing. A fire you can start, move, bank overnight and rebuild is infrastructure. It extends the usable day past sunset, holds predators off, makes a cold night survivable, and — not trivially — creates a fixed place people gather around every evening.
nodes.l3: A hearth is recognisable as a hearth by structure: reddened and cracked sediment beneath, a ring or scatter of stones, ash and charcoal in a bounded shape, and repeated use in the same spot across occupation layers. One burn is a fire; twenty in the same square metre is a hearth.
nodes.ev: Structured hearths; repeated burning in situ

nodes.l1: Using heat to change food before eating it.
nodes.l2: Heat does chemical work that the gut would otherwise have to do: it gelatinises starch, denatures protein, softens tissue and kills parasites. The net effect is more usable energy per bite and less time spent chewing. Cooking also makes some plants edible that are toxic raw, which enlarges the menu considerably.
nodes.l3: Burnt bone and charred plant remains sit in hearth contexts. Dental wear and calculus give an independent line — trapped starch granules in ancient dental plaque can be identified to plant type, and cooked starch looks different from raw under the microscope.
nodes.ev: Charred plant remains; burnt bone; dental calculus
nodes.caution: The 'cooking hypothesis' linking fire to brain expansion is influential but not settled; the timing of the two does not align cleanly.

nodes.l1: The unburnt part of the fire — and a useful substance in its own right.
nodes.l2: Smoke preserves meat and fish by drying them and depositing antimicrobial compounds on the surface. It drives insects out of a shelter. It hardens wood. It is also visible for kilometres, which makes it the first long-distance signal humans could send deliberately.
nodes.l3: Smoke leaves chemical traces. Residue analysis of ceramic and stone surfaces detects combustion products, and soot layers on cave ceilings above hearths record how enclosed spaces were used and ventilated.
nodes.ev: Soot deposits; combustion residues

nodes.l1: Heating a material to change its internal structure, not just its temperature.
nodes.l2: This is the first materials science. Slowly heating silcrete or flint alters its microstructure and makes it flake more predictably — a better tool from the same rock. The insight generalises: heat can change what a substance *is*, not merely warm it. Pottery, metal and glass all live downstream of that idea.
nodes.l3: Heat-treated stone shows a distinctive glossy fracture surface and altered colour, and the change is reproducible in a laboratory. Experimental heating of raw silcrete under controlled conditions produces the same signature found at Middle Stone Age sites in southern Africa.
nodes.ev: Fracture gloss; thermoluminescence; experimental replication

nodes.l1: Doing work on food outside the body so the body has less to do.
nodes.l2: Slicing, pounding and grinding are external digestion. They cut chewing time dramatically and raise the energy actually extracted from a given amount of food. Human jaws, teeth and guts are all small for a primate our size, and processing is the leading explanation for how we get away with that.
nodes.l3: Grinding stones carry use-polish and starch residues. Skeletal evidence runs alongside: reduction in tooth size and jaw robusticity through the genus Homo tracks a diet that needed less mechanical work from the body itself.
nodes.ev: Grinding-stone residues; dental and craniofacial reduction

nodes.l1: Turning a carcass into portable food and raw material.
nodes.l2: Butchery is a sequence, not an act: skin, disarticulate, fillet, crack for marrow. Doing it fast matters when other predators are nearby, and doing it in order matters because each step gives access to the next. A carcass is also hide, sinew, bone and horn — the animal is a materials depot as much as a meal.
nodes.l3: The order of operations is recoverable. Cut-mark position on specific bones indicates which action happened where, and their relationship to carnivore tooth marks — above or below — indicates whether humans or carnivores reached the carcass first.
nodes.ev: Cut-mark position and stratigraphy; bone fragmentation

nodes.l1: Making plants edible by grinding, soaking, leaching or heating them.
nodes.l2: Many of the most abundant plant foods are useless raw. Grains are indigestible without grinding; many tubers and nuts carry toxins that require leaching or heat to remove. Processing converts an inedible but abundant resource into a staple — and staples are what surpluses are made of.
nodes.l3: Starch granules trapped on grinding stones and in dental calculus can be identified to plant species, and processing damages them in characteristic ways. This is how researchers detect cereal use long before any evidence of cultivation.
nodes.ev: Starch granules; grinding-stone use-wear

nodes.l1: Keeping food edible past the moment you acquired it.
nodes.l2: Storage breaks the link between when food is available and when it is eaten, and that changes everything about how people live. It permits staying in one place through a lean season, and it creates something that did not exist before: a stock that can be counted, owned, defended and unequally divided.
nodes.l3: Storage pits, raised granaries and sealed vessels leave structural traces — pit shapes with distinctive fills, post-hole patterns for raised floors that keep rodents out. Phytoliths and residues in pit fills identify what was stored.
nodes.ev: Storage pits; granary post-holes; residue analysis

nodes.l1: People in one place, at the same time, doing nothing urgent.
nodes.l2: A hearth creates a nightly appointment. Firelight extends the day into hours that cannot be used for foraging, and what fills those hours is talk, repair, teaching and story. A great deal of what we call culture needs exactly this: recurring, unhurried, face-to-face time.
nodes.l3: Site structure is the evidence. Artefact scatters around hearths cluster in ways that imply people seated in a ring; different activities leave debris at different distances. Ethnographic studies of contemporary foragers show comparable spatial patterning around fires.
nodes.ev: Spatial artefact patterning around hearths

nodes.l1: Getting something out of one head and into another.
nodes.l2: Communication predates language and is not the same thing. Gesture, expression, vocalisation and demonstration all transfer information. What matters for everything downstream is that information stops dying with the individual who has it.
nodes.l3: There is no direct evidence of speech before writing. Inference runs through anatomy — hyoid bone, vocal tract shape, hearing range — and through behaviour that is hard to coordinate without it. Both lines are indirect and contested.
nodes.ev: Anatomical proxies; behavioural inference
nodes.caution: Claims about the origin of speech rest on indirect proxies. No consensus exists on when language emerged.

nodes.l1: Letting one thing deliberately stand for another.
nodes.l2: A mark that means something is a different order of object from a tool. Once a symbol can carry meaning, meaning becomes storable outside the head and transmissible beyond the people present. Writing, mathematics, money, law and code are all downstream of this single move.
nodes.l3: The Blombos Cave ochre pieces from South Africa carry deliberate cross-hatched engravings roughly 70,000–100,000 years old. Perforated shell beads appear across several regions. What such marks *meant* is unrecoverable; that they were intentional and repeated is not.
nodes.ev: Engraved ochre; perforated shell beads; pigment use
nodes.caution: Marks can be identified as deliberate; their specific meaning cannot be recovered.

nodes.l1: A system where arbitrary sounds combine by rules into unlimited meanings.
nodes.l2: Language is not merely better communication. Its power is recursion and displacement: you can talk about what is not here, what has not happened, and what is not true. Planning a hunt for tomorrow, teaching a technique in the abstract and telling a story all need that.
nodes.l3: Language leaves no direct trace before writing. Everything before that is inference from anatomy, from genetics, and from behaviours that seem to presuppose it. This is one of the genuinely open questions in the field, and honest accounts say so.
nodes.ev: Indirect anatomical, genetic and behavioural inference
nodes.caution: The origin of language is one of the least resolved questions in human evolution. Treat any specific date with suspicion.

nodes.l1: Deliberately structuring what someone else learns.
nodes.l2: Copying is common in the animal world; teaching — where the knowledgeable party changes their own behaviour at a cost to help a learner — is rare. Teaching raises how much skill survives each generational handover, and complex skills only accumulate if the handover loss stays low.
nodes.l3: Experimental studies of stone-tool transmission test this directly: groups are taught knapping by imitation alone, by gesture, or by verbal instruction, and the fidelity of the result is measured. More complex techniques degrade fast without active teaching.
nodes.ev: Transmission-chain experiments; skill-acquisition studies

nodes.l1: Knowledge moving between people and down generations, outside the genes.
nodes.l2: This is the second inheritance system, and it runs far faster than the first. A useful idea can spread through a population within one lifetime and persist for thousands of years. It is the mechanism that makes everything else in this graph possible — nobody rediscovers fire.
nodes.l3: Regional tool traditions that persist across many generations while differing from neighbouring regions are the archaeological signature: the variation is too stable to be individual invention and too localised to be genetic.
nodes.ev: Persistent regional technological traditions

nodes.l1: More understanding held by a group than any member could hold alone.
nodes.l2: Complex technologies exceed what one person can know. A kayak, a bow, a poison, a smelting furnace — each is a long chain of steps refined over generations, where no individual understands the whole and nobody needs to. This is why population size and connectedness affect technological complexity, sometimes more than individual brilliance does.
nodes.l3: Ethnographic and modelling work links group size and inter-group contact to toolkit complexity, and isolated small populations have been observed losing technologies. The generality of the effect is debated, but the mechanism is well described.
nodes.ev: Ethnographic toolkit studies; cultural evolution modelling

nodes.l1: Acting now for a result that arrives later.
nodes.l2: Carrying a tool to a place where you expect to need it is a small act with large implications: it requires modelling a future that does not exist yet. Planning depth is one of the clearer cognitive thresholds visible in the archaeological record, because it shows up as material moved across a landscape.
nodes.l3: Raw-material transport distance is the standard measure. Stone sourced tens or hundreds of kilometres from where it was used implies the toolmaker anticipated future need. Curated, resharpened tools carried between sites tell the same story.
nodes.ev: Raw-material transport distances; tool curation

nodes.l1: Making something whose purpose is not use.
nodes.l2: Art is expensive and does no obvious work, which is exactly why it is informative. Pigment must be sourced, ground and bound; an engraving takes hours. People who were not short of problems spent time on this, which says the output mattered — as identity, as memory, as claim, as meaning.
nodes.l3: Ochre processing kits, engraved objects and pigment-stained tools appear across Africa, Europe and Asia. Uranium-series dating of the calcite crusts over cave paintings gives minimum ages, which is how some European cave art has been pushed back beyond earlier estimates.
nodes.ev: Ochre kits; engraved objects; uranium-series dated pigment

nodes.l1: Repeated action whose value is in the doing, not the outcome.
nodes.l2: Ritual is social technology. Costly, synchronised, repeated behaviour builds trust between people who are not related — and trust between non-relatives is the load-bearing wall of every large society that follows. It is also how knowledge gets encoded in a form people rehearse rather than merely remember.
nodes.l3: Deliberate burial with grave goods, arranged non-utilitarian objects, and structures with no practical function are the usual signatures. Each is contested individually, since a burial may be hygiene and an arrangement may be chance, but the pattern across sites is harder to dismiss.
nodes.ev: Deliberate burials; grave goods; non-utilitarian structures
nodes.caution: Individual claims of ritual behaviour — especially for Neanderthals — are frequently disputed on taphonomic grounds.

nodes.l1: Images placed deliberately in deep, dark, hard-to-reach spaces.
nodes.l2: Cave art is not decoration — decoration goes where people live. These images are often hundreds of metres inside, in chambers reachable only by crawling, visible only by carried firelight. Somebody planned a lighting system, an expedition and a composition, and the result was meant to be seen by few.
nodes.l3: Uranium-series dating of overlying calcite gives minimum ages. Charcoal in the pigment itself can be radiocarbon dated. Sites in Europe and in Sulawesi, Indonesia, both yield very early dates, which undercuts any single-origin story for figurative image-making.
nodes.ev: Uranium-series and radiocarbon dating; pigment analysis
nodes.caution: Figurative cave art appears independently in widely separated regions; a single European origin is not supported.

nodes.l1: Knowing a territory well enough to predict what it will offer, and when.
nodes.l2: A landscape held in the head is a map of water, stone sources, seasonal fruiting, animal routes and safe crossings. It is the difference between wandering and moving with intent, and it is knowledge that only pays off over years — which means it has to be transmitted, not learned fresh.
nodes.l3: Raw-material sourcing is the hard evidence. Geochemical fingerprinting matches stone artefacts to specific outcrops, letting archaeologists map the territory a group actually used. Some assemblages contain material from several hundred kilometres away.
nodes.ev: Geochemical sourcing of lithic raw material

nodes.l1: Following the year around a territory rather than staying put.
nodes.l2: Resources are not evenly distributed in time. A group that moves on a schedule tuned to fruiting, spawning and migration harvests the peak of each rather than the average of one place. It is a strategy that requires knowing the calendar of a landscape before the calendar exists.
nodes.l3: Seasonality is read from remains that grew in a known season: fish otoliths and shellfish shells lay down growth rings, and tooth cementum in mammals bands annually. These indicate the season of death, so a site can be shown to have been occupied only in autumn, or only in spring.
nodes.ev: Growth-increment seasonality; site occupation patterns

nodes.l1: Several people acting on one intention that none of them holds alone.
nodes.l2: Human cooperation is unusual in scale and in who it includes. Most animals cooperate with kin; humans cooperate routinely with strangers, sustained by reputation, reciprocity and shared norms rather than relatedness. Every institution later in this graph is an attempt to make that work at larger scale.
nodes.l3: Cooperation is visible archaeologically as tasks no individual could complete: large-game drives, structures needing many hands, and the movement of material through exchange networks between groups.
nodes.ev: Communal hunting sites; exchange networks; large structures

nodes.l1: Moving into land where nobody you know has ever lived.
nodes.l2: Humans occupied nearly every terrestrial environment on the planet without evolving specialised bodies for any of them. That is a technological and cultural achievement rather than a biological one — clothing, fire, shelter and transmitted local knowledge did the work that fur and fat do for other species.
nodes.l3: Genetics and archaeology are now read together. Ancient DNA from human remains reconstructs population movement and mixture directly, and it has repeatedly overturned tidy migration stories built on artefact styles alone.
nodes.ev: Ancient DNA; dated site sequences; artefact distributions
nodes.caution: Migration routes and dates are revised frequently as ancient DNA accumulates. Treat any specific route as provisional.

nodes.l1: Solving a climate with equipment instead of with a body.
nodes.l2: Adapting culturally is far faster than adapting genetically — a new garment design spreads in a generation, a new metabolism takes thousands. This is the central reason a single species with almost no anatomical variation occupies the Arctic, the Sahara and the high Andes at once.
nodes.l3: Cold-climate occupation leaves a distinctive toolkit: eyed needles, insulated dwellings, fuel management, fat-rendering equipment. Sites at high latitude and altitude are dated to show when each threshold was crossed.
nodes.ev: Cold-climate toolkits; high-latitude site dating

nodes.l1: Getting to the other side of water you cannot wade or swim.
nodes.l2: Water is the hardest barrier on a map, and crossing it opens land nobody else has claimed. Reaching Australia required open-sea voyages of tens of kilometres, across water that was never dry even at lowest sea level — which makes it the earliest strong evidence for watercraft anywhere.
nodes.l3: The reasoning here is geographic rather than artefactual: no boat survives, but sea-level reconstruction shows the gaps that had to be crossed, and dated occupation on the far side shows they were. Absence of the vessel does not weaken the inference.
nodes.ev: Palaeo-sea-level reconstruction; dated island occupation

nodes.l1: Buoyant material tied together until it carries weight.
nodes.l2: A raft floats by displacement and needs no hull, no shaping and no watertight joint — which makes it the lowest-technology way to move mass across water. It is slow and hard to steer, and it still changes what is reachable, especially along rivers and coasts.
nodes.l3: Direct evidence is essentially nil; organic craft do not survive. Experimental voyages using period-plausible materials test whether particular crossings were feasible, which constrains the possibilities without proving any one case.
nodes.ev: Experimental voyaging; inference from island colonisation
nodes.caution: No prehistoric raft survives. Reconstructions are plausibility tests, not artefacts.

nodes.l1: A shaped hull that displaces water and keeps its cargo dry.
nodes.l2: A hull can be steered, loaded and driven against a current in ways a raft cannot. Boats make rivers into roads. For most of history, moving goods by water was an order of magnitude cheaper than moving them by land, which is why almost every early city sits on a waterway.
nodes.l3: The Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, a hollowed pine log roughly 10,000 years old, is among the oldest surviving boats. Waterlogged burial preserved it. Earlier watercraft are inferred from island settlement rather than recovered.
nodes.ev: Waterlogged dugout finds; island colonisation dates

nodes.l1: Knowing where you are and which way to go with no landmarks in sight.
nodes.l2: Open water removes every reference a land animal uses. Navigators replaced them with star paths, swell direction, cloud behaviour over unseen islands and bird flight — a system held entirely in memory and taught by apprenticeship. Pacific voyagers crossed thousands of kilometres of ocean this way.
nodes.l3: Pacific navigation traditions were documented ethnographically while still practised, and have been tested by instrument-free voyages on reconstructed craft. Settlement chronologies across Oceania independently confirm the routes.
nodes.ev: Documented navigational traditions; instrument-free voyages

nodes.l1: Nets, weirs, traps and hooks — catching more than you could by hand.
nodes.l2: A net turns fishing from an individual pursuit into a harvest, and a fixed weir turns it into infrastructure that works while you sleep. This is the point where an aquatic food source becomes reliable enough to build a settled life around, sometimes long before farming.
nodes.l3: Fish weirs survive as stake alignments in waterlogged ground and can be radiocarbon dated. Net sinkers, shell hooks and mass fish-bone deposits in middens show scale of catch rather than mere presence.
nodes.ev: Dated fish weirs; net weights; midden fish assemblages

nodes.l1: A dwelling built to outlast the season.
nodes.l2: Building for permanence changes the economics of effort. A structure you will return to is worth a stone footing, a dug floor and a proper hearth — investments that make no sense in a shelter you abandon in a week. Permanence also makes possessions worth having, since they no longer have to be carried.
nodes.l3: Substantial construction shows as dug floors, stone foundations, heavy post-holes, repeated re-flooring and thick occupation deposits. Depth of accumulation distinguishes long residence from repeated brief visits.
nodes.ev: Dug floors; stone footings; deep occupation deposits

nodes.l1: Staying in one place long enough that the place becomes yours.
nodes.l2: Sedentism preceded farming in several regions rather than following it — where wild resources were rich and predictable enough, people settled first and cultivated later. Once settled, birth spacing shortens, possessions accumulate, refuse becomes a problem and land becomes something to hold.
nodes.l3: Sedentism is inferred from a bundle: heavy immovable equipment such as grinding slabs, year-round seasonality indicators, commensal animals like house mice and sparrows, and deep midden accumulation.
nodes.ev: Immovable equipment; year-round seasonality; commensal species
nodes.caution: Settlement did not always follow agriculture. In several regions the sequence runs the other way.

nodes.l1: More people, packed more densely, than mobile life allows.
nodes.l2: Settled life shortens the interval between births, because a mother no longer has to carry each child across a landscape. Denser populations mean more minds and more hands — and also crowd diseases, more conflict over land, and a much harder floor to fall back to if the harvest fails.
nodes.l3: Population is estimated from settlement area and house counts, and cross-checked against skeletal indicators of health and stress. The skeletal record often shows declining stature and increased disease markers with early farming, alongside rising numbers.
nodes.ev: Settlement-size estimates; palaeodemography; skeletal stress markers
nodes.caution: More people is not the same as better off. Early farming populations frequently show worse individual health than the foragers they replaced.

nodes.l1: Different people doing different work, and trading the results.
nodes.l2: Specialisation raises skill because practice concentrates, and it raises output because switching costs disappear. It also creates dependency: a full-time potter does not grow food and will starve without someone who does. Every complex society is a machine for managing that mutual dependency.
nodes.l3: Craft specialisation shows as standardised output — vessels of consistent form and fabric, produced in quantity, in workshop areas with production debris. Skeletal markers of repetitive occupational stress point the same way.
nodes.ev: Standardised craft output; workshop debris; occupational skeletal markers

nodes.l1: Deciding who gets what, and keeping some back for later.
nodes.l2: A stored surplus has to be governed. Who may draw on it, how much is held for seed, what happens in a bad year — these are questions with no natural answer, and the ways societies answered them became the first institutions. Management of stock is where politics starts.
nodes.l3: Communal storage facilities, standardised measuring vessels and — later — accounting tokens indicate deliberate allocation. Placement of granaries, whether in individual houses or in a shared central structure, distinguishes household from communal control.
nodes.ev: Communal granaries; standard measures; accounting tokens

nodes.l1: Knowing which plants feed you, which cure you, and which kill you.
nodes.l2: Foraging societies routinely command detailed knowledge of hundreds of species — where each grows, when it ripens, how it must be processed, what it treats. This body of knowledge is the entire precondition for agriculture. Nobody domesticates a plant they do not already understand.
nodes.l3: Starch and phytolith residues on tools, plant remains in hearths and dental calculus, and coprolite analysis together reconstruct the plant component of ancient diets — a component the bone-heavy record systematically undercounts.
nodes.ev: Phytoliths; starch residues; dental calculus; coprolites

nodes.l1: Keeping the best seed to plant rather than eating it.
nodes.l2: This is a genuinely difficult decision: setting aside good food now for a benefit that arrives months later and may not arrive at all. Repeated over generations, it also does something nobody intended — it changes the plant, selecting for larger grain and for seed heads that stay attached instead of shattering.
nodes.l3: Domestication is visible in the seeds themselves. Grain size increases and the rachis — the attachment point — becomes tough rather than brittle. Both changes are measurable in charred assemblages, and they appear gradually over centuries.
nodes.ev: Grain-size series; rachis morphology in charred assemblages

nodes.l1: Deliberately making a place better for the plants you want.
nodes.l2: Cultivation starts long before domestication: clearing competitors, watering, burning to encourage regrowth, sowing gathered seed. It is a spectrum of intervention, not a switch, which is why 'the invention of agriculture' is a misleading phrase for a process that took thousands of years.
nodes.l3: Weed floras give it away. Cultivated ground supports a distinctive community of disturbance-loving species, and their appearance in archaeobotanical assemblages signals tillage before the crops themselves show domestication traits.
nodes.ev: Arable weed assemblages; field systems; tillage marks

nodes.date: ≈ 11,000 years ago onward, independently in several regions
nodes.l1: A species reshaped by living alongside humans, over generations.
nodes.l2: Domestication is mutual. Humans changed wheat, cattle, rice, maize and dogs; those species changed human diet, settlement, labour and disease exposure in return. It happened independently in at least eleven regions with different species — which makes it a repeated response to conditions, not a single invention that spread.
nodes.l3: Morphological change is visible in bones and seeds; genomic change is now readable directly from ancient DNA, which can date and locate domestication events and detect the repeated mixing between wild and domestic populations.
nodes.ev: Morphological change; ancient genomes; regional chronologies
nodes.caution: Domestication arose independently in multiple regions. There is no single origin point, and no evidence of a plan.

nodes.l1: Managing animals on the hoof instead of hunting them.
nodes.l2: A herd is a food store that walks. It converts grass — which humans cannot eat — into milk, meat, hide, wool and traction, and it can be moved to land too dry or steep to farm. Herding also brings people into close, permanent contact with animals, with consequences for disease that nobody anticipated.
nodes.l3: Kill-off patterns are the key: hunted populations show a natural age spread, managed ones show culling of young males and retention of females. Lipid residues in pots detect dairying directly, and the human genetics of lactase persistence tracks it independently.
nodes.ev: Age-at-death profiles; dairy lipid residues; lactase persistence genetics

nodes.l1: Sickles, hoes, digging sticks, ards — equipment for working soil and harvest.
nodes.l2: The tools set the ceiling on how much land one household can work, and that ceiling sets everything else: surplus, population, how many people can do something other than farm. Later, the shift from hand tools to animal traction raises the ceiling again by roughly an order of magnitude.
nodes.l3: Sickle blades develop a characteristic silica gloss from cutting cereal stems, identifiable under magnification. Ard marks survive as crossed scratch patterns preserved in buried soils beneath later monuments.
nodes.ev: Sickle gloss; preserved ard marks; tool assemblages

nodes.l1: Moving water to where the crops are.
nodes.l2: Irrigation makes dry land productive and decouples the harvest from rainfall. It is also the first technology that forces collective organisation: canals must be dug by many, maintained forever, and shared under rules. Some of the earliest written records anywhere are water allocation disputes.
nodes.l3: Canal systems survive as earthworks and are datable by their fills. Salinisation — the accumulation of salt that eventually ruins irrigated soil — is detectable in sediments and in a shift in crops from wheat to more salt-tolerant barley.
nodes.ev: Canal earthworks; sediment salinisation; crop-shift records
nodes.caution: Irrigation can degrade the land it feeds. Salinisation is documented in several early systems.

nodes.l1: Keeping a harvest dry, sealed and safe from rodents until next year.
nodes.l2: Grain stores well, which is exactly why it became the staple of state societies rather than more nutritious but perishable crops. A sealed granary holds a year of food, and a countable, taxable, seizable asset. It is hard to overstate how much of subsequent history follows from that property.
nodes.l3: Granaries appear as raised structures on post settings — the elevation keeps rodents out and air moving. Some at Pre-Pottery Neolithic sites in the Jordan Valley predate clear crop domestication, meaning storage came first.
nodes.ev: Raised granary structures; storage pits; sealed vessels

nodes.date: ≈ 11,000 years ago, independently in multiple regions
nodes.l1: Producing food deliberately instead of finding it.
nodes.l2: Agriculture raises calories per hectare enormously and lowers them per hour worked — farmers generally work harder than foragers for a less varied diet. What it buys is density and storability, and those two properties support everything that needs a lot of people in one place: cities, states, specialists, writing.
nodes.l3: Independent origins are documented in Southwest Asia, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea and elsewhere, each with different crops on different timelines. Charred plant assemblages, isotopes and ancient genomes converge on the same picture.
nodes.ev: Regional archaeobotanical sequences; isotopes; crop genomes
nodes.caution: Agriculture was not a single invention that spread from one place, and it was not obviously an improvement for the individuals who adopted it.

nodes.l1: More food than the people who grew it need to eat.
nodes.l2: Surplus is the hinge of this whole section. It is what pays for people who do not farm — priests, potters, soldiers, scribes, engineers — and therefore what makes specialisation, hierarchy and cities structurally possible. It is also the thing that can be taken, which is where states begin.
nodes.l3: Surplus is inferred from storage capacity relative to estimated population, and from the presence of full-time specialists who must have been fed by someone else. Later, written ration and tax records make it explicit.
nodes.ev: Storage-capacity estimates; specialist populations; ration records

nodes.l1: Treating ground as a divisible, ownable, improvable asset.
nodes.l2: Once land is improved — cleared, terraced, irrigated, manured — the improvement has to be defended, which turns territory into property. Fallow rotation, terracing and manuring are the techniques; boundaries, inheritance and land law are the institutions that grew around them.
nodes.l3: Field systems survive as boundary banks, walls and terraces, mappable from the air and from lidar. Manuring is detectable as scatters of domestic pottery spread across fields with the muck.
nodes.ev: Field boundaries; terraces; manuring scatters; lidar survey

nodes.l1: Enough households in one place that they must agree on rules.
nodes.l2: A village crosses a threshold that a camp does not: you now live permanently among people you did not choose and cannot avoid. Shared walls, shared water, shared waste and shared defence all need conventions, and the conventions need enforcement. Village life is where most social institutions were first worked out.
nodes.l3: Sites such as Çatalhöyük in Anatolia show dense agglomerated housing over many rebuild phases, with household-level storage and burial beneath floors — a settlement that is clearly permanent and clearly organised, but with no obvious central authority.
nodes.ev: Agglomerated house plans; rebuild sequences; household storage

nodes.l1: A village organised around a shared agricultural calendar.
nodes.l2: Farming synchronises people. Ploughing, sowing and harvest have narrow windows, and missing one costs a year — so labour must be pooled at exactly the same moments. That shared calendar becomes the backbone of communal ritual, obligation and, eventually, the formal year.
nodes.l3: Communal structures, shared threshing floors and standardised house layouts indicate coordination. Seasonal ritual sites aligned to solstices tie the agricultural calendar to the astronomical one.
nodes.ev: Communal facilities; standardised layouts; solstice alignments

nodes.l1: People who do one thing full-time and eat because others farm.
nodes.l2: Full-time specialists are where skill compounds. A potter who throws every day for thirty years reaches a level no part-timer reaches, and the same holds for metalworkers, scribes and builders. Every technically demanding object later in this graph implies somebody was fed to make it.
nodes.l3: Workshop areas with concentrated production debris, highly standardised products and specialist-only tools mark the transition. Burials with craft toolkits identify individuals by trade.
nodes.ev: Workshop debris; product standardisation; craft-tool burials

nodes.l1: Goods moving between people who each want what the other has.
nodes.l2: Trade lets a region use resources it does not have, and it moves ideas along with cargo — techniques, styles, scripts and diseases all travel the same routes. Long-distance exchange networks existed long before states, and they are among the best evidence that unrelated groups could sustain trust.
nodes.l3: Provenance science makes trade visible. Obsidian is geochemically fingerprinted to specific volcanic sources, so a blade found hundreds of kilometres away proves a route. Lead isotopes do the same for metals, amber and shell for other networks.
nodes.ev: Obsidian sourcing; lead-isotope provenance; exotic goods distribution

nodes.l1: Clay heated until it stops being clay and becomes ceramic.
nodes.l2: Firing is irreversible chemistry: above roughly 600 °C the clay minerals lose their bound water and cannot be re-softened. That gives waterproof, rot-proof, insect-proof containers — and containers are what let you store liquid, boil food, ship oil and count a harvest. Pottery is also the archaeologist's clock, because styles change fast and sherds survive forever.
nodes.l3: Ceramics are dated by thermoluminescence, which measures the energy accumulated since the last firing. Fabric analysis identifies clay sources; residue analysis of absorbed lipids reveals what a pot actually held.
nodes.ev: Thermoluminescence dating; fabric sourcing; absorbed lipid residues
nodes.caution: Pottery predates farming in some regions — East Asian hunter-gatherer ceramics are considerably older than Southwest Asian farming ones.

nodes.l1: A standard unit of building, made from mud where there is no stone.
nodes.l2: The brick is arguably the first mass-produced standardised object. Identical modules mean a wall can be built by many hands without individual fitting, and it means the design can be planned before the material exists. Mesopotamian civilisation was built almost entirely from mud brick because it had abundant clay and almost no stone.
nodes.l3: Brick dimensions are recorded and compared across sites and periods; standard sizes changed in ways precise enough to help date a structure. Mud-brick collapse creates the characteristic layered mounds — tells — that mark long-occupied Near Eastern sites.
nodes.ev: Standardised brick dimensions; tell stratigraphy

nodes.l1: Assembling material into a structure that stays up.
nodes.l2: Building large means solving for loads that will not forgive a mistake, and organising labour that must arrive in the right order. Göbekli Tepe in Turkey shows monumental stone construction around 11,000 years ago — before farming was established there, which upends the assumption that surplus must come first and monuments second.
nodes.l3: Construction sequence is recovered from quarry marks, tool traces, ramp remains and the stratigraphy of building phases. Experimental archaeology tests how many people and how long a given method would take.
nodes.ev: Quarry and tool marks; construction ramps; build phasing
nodes.caution: Göbekli Tepe suggests monumental construction can precede agriculture, reversing a long-assumed sequence.

nodes.l1: Building designed before it is built, to mean something as well as stand up.
nodes.l2: Architecture is construction plus intention. A temple is not larger than it needs to be by accident — scale, alignment, approach and sightline are used deliberately to produce an effect on the person walking in. It is one of the oldest technologies for making a large group feel something at once.
nodes.l3: Plans exist. Mesopotamian and Egyptian architectural drawings, scale models and written specifications survive, and building alignments can be checked against solar and stellar positions for the relevant period.
nodes.ev: Ancient plans and models; astronomical alignments; standing structures

nodes.l1: A prepared surface that makes travel predictable.
nodes.l2: Roads compress distance. They cut transport cost and time, which enlarges the area a single authority can govern, an army can reach and a market can serve. Almost every empire in history is partly a road network — the political map tends to stop where the roads do.
nodes.l3: Road surfaces, kerbs and cuttings survive and are excavated directly. Milestones and itineraries give named routes and distances. Wheel ruts worn into stone record gauge and traffic volume.
nodes.ev: Excavated road surfaces; milestones; wheel ruts

nodes.l1: Deciding the shape of a settlement before people live in it.
nodes.l2: A planned city is an argument about how life should be organised, executed in stone and drainage. Grid streets, zoned quarters, standardised housing and centralised water are all decisions imposed in advance — which means somebody had both the authority to impose them and a model of the city in mind.
nodes.l3: Indus Valley cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa show grid layouts, standardised brick ratios and covered drainage across the whole settlement. Uniformity at that scale is not emergent; it is administered.
nodes.ev: Grid layouts; standardised brick ratios; city-wide drainage

nodes.l1: Bigger than a village, and no longer feeding itself.
nodes.l2: A town is the point at which a settlement stops being agricultural and starts being a node — it lives off exchange, craft and administration, drawing food from a hinterland. That dependence is a structural vulnerability as much as an achievement.
nodes.l3: Regional survey maps settlement hierarchies: many small sites, fewer medium ones, a handful of large ones. That distribution is itself the evidence of a town-and-hinterland economy.
nodes.ev: Regional settlement-hierarchy survey; craft concentration

nodes.l1: Enough people in one place that most of them are strangers.
nodes.l2: Anonymity is the defining feature. In a village, behaviour is regulated by everyone knowing everyone; in a city that mechanism fails, and something else must replace it — written law, contracts, currency, police, formal institutions. Cities are also where ideas meet, which is why they produce disproportionate innovation and disproportionate disease.
nodes.l3: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia is among the earliest, with monumental architecture, mass-produced ration bowls and the earliest known writing. Population estimates come from built area and household density, with wide error bars.
nodes.ev: Uruk excavations; built-area demography; administrative records

nodes.l1: Somebody who can make a decision that binds everyone else.
nodes.l2: Government is the answer to problems too large for negotiation: defence, irrigation, famine reserve, dispute settlement between strangers. It is also, immediately and everywhere, a mechanism for extraction. Both faces appear together in the record; neither is a later corruption of the other.
nodes.l3: Administrative seals, standardised ration containers, monumental construction requiring coordinated labour, and elite burials with restricted goods all indicate centralised authority before any text describes it.
nodes.ev: Administrative sealings; ration standardisation; elite burials

nodes.l1: Rules written down so they outlive the person who made them.
nodes.l2: An unwritten rule is whatever the powerful person says it is today. Writing a rule down and displaying it publicly does something structurally different: it makes the rule checkable, and it binds the ruler to their own past statement. That is a real constraint even when it is frequently ignored.
nodes.l3: The Code of Ur-Nammu and the later Code of Hammurabi survive as inscribed stone and clay. Alongside the codes sit thousands of ordinary court records and contracts, which show how law was actually applied rather than merely proclaimed.
nodes.ev: Inscribed law codes; court records; contracts

nodes.l1: Running a society by paperwork rather than by personal presence.
nodes.l2: Beyond a few thousand people, a ruler cannot personally know what is happening. Administration substitutes records for presence: lists, receipts, inventories, personnel rolls. It is unglamorous and it is the actual machinery of every large state — most surviving cuneiform is not literature but accounts.
nodes.l3: Archives of administrative tablets survive in tens of thousands from Mesopotamian and Egyptian sites, recording rations, livestock, labour rosters and land. They are the most abundant written source from the ancient world.
nodes.ev: Administrative tablet archives; sealings; inventories

nodes.l1: A share of what you produce, taken by an authority.
nodes.l2: Taxation converts a diffuse surplus into a concentrated one that can be spent on armies, monuments, canals and scribes. It requires knowing what exists and who owns it — which is why the state's need to tax has driven the development of measurement, census, cadastral survey and writing itself.
nodes.l3: Tax assessments, receipts and exemption grants survive in quantity. Egyptian records of Nile flood height used to predict yield and set tax rates are a striking case of measurement in the service of extraction.
nodes.ev: Tax receipts and assessments; Nilometer records; cadastral survey

nodes.l1: Language made visible, durable and separable from the speaker.
nodes.l2: Writing detaches a message from the presence of the person who made it. It can outlive them, travel without them and be checked against later. Everything that depends on accumulating knowledge across generations rather than within a lifetime — law, science, contract, history — sits on top of that one property.
nodes.l3: Cuneiform's development is unusually well documented, because it begins as an accounting system and gradually becomes general-purpose. The earliest tablets from Uruk record commodities and quantities; the abstraction to full language takes centuries.
nodes.ev: Uruk proto-cuneiform tablets; script development sequences
nodes.caution: Writing was invented independently at least three or four times — Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica — with different mechanisms and no shared origin.

nodes.l1: Storing a quantity outside anyone's memory.
nodes.l2: Records came before writing. Clay tokens representing commodities were sealed in containers, and marks pressed on the outside noted what was inside. This is the actual ancestor of the script — writing seems to have grown out of the need to count things reliably, not out of a wish to tell stories.
nodes.l3: Token systems are found across the Near East over several millennia, followed by sealed clay envelopes, then impressed tablets, then signs. The sequence is materially continuous, which is why the accounting-origin argument for writing is well supported.
nodes.ev: Clay token systems; sealed bullae; impressed tablets

nodes.l1: Symbols for quantity that can be combined by rules.
nodes.l2: A notation is not just shorthand — it determines what calculations are practical. Positional notation with a zero makes long multiplication and division routine; Roman numerals make them a specialist skill. The tool for thinking shapes what gets thought.
nodes.l3: Mesopotamian scribes used base-60 positional notation, which survives in our minutes, seconds and degrees. Mathematical tablets show multiplication tables, reciprocals and problem sets — teaching material, complete with student errors.
nodes.ev: Cuneiform mathematical tablets; numeral systems across scripts

nodes.l1: Keeping track of who owes what to whom.
nodes.l2: Accounting is the technology that lets economic relationships outlive memory and trust. Once obligation is recorded, it can be transferred, enforced and audited — and credit becomes possible between people who have no reason to trust each other. Most early writing is accounting, which says something about priorities.
nodes.l3: Token systems, then tablets, record quantities, commodities, parties and dates. Double-entry bookkeeping appears much later, formalised in fifteenth-century Italy, and transforms what can be tracked in a complex business.
nodes.ev: Accounting tablets; token systems; later double-entry manuals

nodes.l1: Dividing time into named units that repeat.
nodes.l2: Farming needs to know when to plant, and ritual needs to know when to gather. Both require predicting a date months ahead, which means modelling the sky. The awkward part is that the solar year, lunar month and day do not divide evenly into each other — every calendar in history is a different compromise with that fact.
nodes.l3: Calendrical texts, intercalation records — inserted extra months to keep drift in check — and monument alignments to solstice or heliacal risings all survive. The Mesoamerican Long Count and Egyptian civil calendar show independent solutions to the same arithmetic problem.
nodes.ev: Calendrical texts; intercalation records; monument alignments

nodes.date: ≈ 4,000 years ago onward as systematic record
nodes.l1: Watching the sky carefully enough to predict it.
nodes.l2: Astronomy is where prediction was invented. Babylonian scribes kept nightly records for centuries and found that eclipses recur in cycles — meaning a future event could be forecast from past data alone, without any theory of why. That is the template for empirical science, arrived at through the sky because the sky is the one system that repeats reliably.
nodes.l3: Babylonian astronomical diaries span many centuries of continuous observation and survive on clay. Their eclipse records are precise enough that modern astronomers use them to measure the long-term slowing of Earth's rotation.
nodes.ev: Babylonian astronomical diaries; eclipse records; alignments

nodes.l1: A whole system of production, exchange and obligation, larger than anyone in it.
nodes.l2: Once exchange, credit, taxation and specialised production interlock, the result behaves as a system with its own dynamics — prices, shortages, booms and crashes that nobody chose. Ancient records include price series, interest rates, debt and periodic debt cancellation, which suggests the instabilities were recognised early.
nodes.l3: Price and wage series reconstructed from Mesopotamian and Egyptian records allow economic history well before coinage. Debt-remission edicts are direct evidence that debt accumulation was a recurring structural problem.
nodes.ev: Ancient price series; interest and debt records; remission edicts

nodes.l1: Cities, writing, specialists and institutions, interlocking.
nodes.l2: The word carries baggage worth naming: it has often been used to rank societies, with the ranking following whoever was doing the ranking. As a descriptive term for a particular configuration — dense urban settlement, record-keeping, occupational specialisation, formal institutions — it is useful. As a judgement of worth, it has a poor record.
nodes.l3: The configuration appears independently in Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley, China, Mesoamerica and the Andes, with different crops, scripts, architecture and beliefs. The recurrence of the pattern is the interesting finding; the ranking of the instances is not a scientific question.
nodes.ev: Independent regional sequences; comparative archaeology
nodes.caution: 'Civilisation' has a long history of use as a value judgement ranking peoples. Used here strictly as a description of a social configuration.

nodes.l1: The first metal worked at scale — soft, red, and reshapeable without breaking.
nodes.l2: Copper introduces a property no earlier material had: it deforms without fracturing, and it can be melted and recast indefinitely. A broken stone tool is gone; a broken copper tool is raw material. That single fact changes how tools are valued, repaired and inherited.
nodes.l3: Lead isotope analysis fingerprints copper to its ore source, mapping ancient metal trade across regions. Native copper artefacts predate smelting and are identifiable by their worked-but-unmelted microstructure.
nodes.ev: Lead-isotope provenance; metallography; slag and crucible finds

nodes.l1: Extracting metal from rock that does not look remotely like metal.
nodes.l2: Smelting is a conceptual leap larger than it appears. Green malachite ore looks nothing like copper, and getting one from the other requires high temperature *and* a reducing atmosphere — starving the fire of oxygen so carbon monoxide strips oxygen from the ore. Both conditions must hold at once, and neither is obvious.
nodes.l3: Smelting sites are identified by slag — the glassy waste with a distinctive chemistry — plus furnace remains, tuyère fragments from bellows, and crucibles. Slag composition reveals furnace temperature and atmosphere.
nodes.ev: Slag chemistry; furnace and tuyère remains; crucibles
nodes.caution: Kiln technology developed for pottery plausibly supplied the temperature control smelting needs, but a direct causal link is inferred rather than documented.

nodes.l1: Copper deliberately mixed with tin to make something better than either.
nodes.l2: Bronze is the first engineered alloy: harder than copper, lower melting point, casts more cleanly. It also has an awkward property — tin is rare and rarely found near copper, so bronze forces long-distance trade. Bronze Age economies were bound together by a supply chain, and were vulnerable when it broke.
nodes.l3: Alloy composition is measured directly by spectrometry, and tin content proves deliberate alloying rather than accidental ore mixing. Shipwreck cargoes such as Uluburun preserve ingots in transit and map the trade.
nodes.ev: Alloy composition analysis; ingot cargoes; shipwreck assemblages

nodes.l1: Cast, sharpened, resharpened, and eventually melted down and recast.
nodes.l2: Bronze tools hold an edge far better than copper and can be produced to a consistent shape by casting from a mould. Casting is the key: it turns toolmaking from individual craft into repeatable production, and it makes complex shapes — sockets, hollow forms — that no stone tool could take.
nodes.l3: Moulds survive in stone and clay, and casting seams on finished objects match them. Recycling is visible chemically, because remelted bronze accumulates a mixed impurity signature.
nodes.ev: Casting moulds; casting seams; recycling signatures

nodes.l1: Common, cheap, and much harder to work than bronze.
nodes.l2: Iron ore is everywhere, which is its whole advantage — no trade route required. The problem is that iron melts far above the temperature ancient furnaces reached, so early ironworking produced a spongy solid bloom that had to be hammered while hot to drive out slag. More labour, worse initial product, vastly better supply.
nodes.l3: Bloomery slag differs chemically from copper slag and is abundant at ironworking sites. Metallography of finished objects reveals forging history in the grain structure, including how many times a piece was folded and welded.
nodes.ev: Bloomery slag; metallographic grain structure; forge sites
nodes.caution: Iron replaced bronze because of supply, not because early iron was a better material. The first iron tools were often inferior.

nodes.l1: Hammering hot iron into shape, over and over.
nodes.l2: Because iron could not be melted and poured, it had to be forged — heated to red heat and beaten, repeatedly, to consolidate the metal and expel slag. Folding and welding distributes carbon and impurities more evenly, and the resulting layered structure is both stronger and, in some traditions, visibly patterned.
nodes.l3: Grain structure and slag-stringer patterns in cross-sections record the forging sequence. Experimental smithing reproduces the signatures and calibrates how much work each stage represents.
nodes.ev: Metallography; slag inclusions; experimental smithing

nodes.date: Ancient in small quantities; industrial from 1856
nodes.l1: Iron with a precisely controlled trace of carbon — around one part in a hundred.
nodes.l2: A very small amount of carbon transforms iron's mechanical behaviour: hard enough to hold an edge, tough enough not to shatter. Ancient smiths achieved it by skill and feel. Bessemer's converter in 1856 achieved it by process control, and cheap bulk steel is the material that rails, ships, skyscrapers and machine tools are made of.
nodes.l3: Carbon content and heat-treatment history are readable from microstructure. The Bessemer process is documented in patents, plant records and production statistics, and the resulting collapse in steel prices is visible in economic series.
nodes.ev: Microstructure analysis; patents and plant records; price series

nodes.date: Practical for millennia; theoretical from the 1800s
nodes.l1: Understanding metals well enough to design one for a job.
nodes.l2: For most of history metallurgy was inherited procedure — do exactly this and it works, nobody knows why. Understanding why, through phase diagrams and crystal structure, converted it into design: specify the properties you need, then choose the composition and heat treatment that deliver them. That shift underlies every modern engineered material.
nodes.l3: Ancient practice is reconstructed from workshop remains and object analysis. Modern metallurgy is documented in the phase diagrams, crystallographic studies and standards that let alloys be specified and reproduced anywhere.
nodes.ev: Workshop archaeology; phase diagrams; materials standards

nodes.l1: Shaping metal by hitting it, usually hot.
nodes.l2: Forging does more than change shape. Working metal deforms its grain structure and hardens it, and hot working lets it be reshaped without cracking. A forged component is generally stronger than a cast one of the same alloy because the grain flow follows the part's geometry.
nodes.l3: Hammer marks survive on unfinished work, and grain flow in cross-section distinguishes forged from cast components. Anvils, tongs and hearth remains identify smithies archaeologically.
nodes.ev: Hammer marks; grain-flow metallography; smithy remains

nodes.l1: Pouring liquid metal into a shaped cavity and letting it solidify.
nodes.l2: Casting decouples the complexity of a shape from the difficulty of making it. Once a mould exists, a complicated form costs the same as a simple one, and it can be repeated exactly. Lost-wax casting can reproduce a modelled original in metal at full detail — a capability that runs from ancient bronzes to modern turbine blades.
nodes.l3: Moulds, crucibles and sprues survive, and casting flaws — porosity, cold shuts, seams — identify the technique in finished objects. Lost-wax work is recognisable because the object has no mould seam and no draft angle.
nodes.ev: Moulds and crucibles; casting flaws; absence of mould seams

nodes.l1: A disc that turns on a fixed centre, converting drag into rolling.
nodes.l2: The wheel is famously counter-intuitive as an invention because it is useless alone. It needs a low-friction axle bearing, a hard enough material for both, and a prepared surface to run on — which is why it appears late, and why several sophisticated societies never adopted it for transport. It is not obvious, and it is not always the best answer.
nodes.l3: The earliest evidence includes potter's wheels, model wagons, wheel ruts and actual wooden wheels preserved in waterlogged conditions, appearing across Mesopotamia and Europe within a few centuries of each other.
nodes.ev: Preserved wooden wheels; wagon models; wheel ruts; pictographs
nodes.caution: Mesoamerican societies knew the wheel — it appears on toys — but lacked draught animals, so it was not used for transport. Absence is not ignorance.

nodes.l1: The fixed shaft a wheel turns around. The hard half of the problem.
nodes.l2: The wheel is easy; the bearing is not. The axle must carry the full load while allowing rotation, with tolerances tight enough to avoid wobble and loose enough to avoid seizing, and it wears constantly. Most of the engineering history of the wheel is actually the history of bearings and lubrication.
nodes.l3: Wear patterns on surviving axles and hubs record load and lubrication. Some early designs rotate the axle with the wheels; others fix it — the two solutions leave different wear signatures.
nodes.ev: Axle and hub wear analysis; surviving wagon components

nodes.l1: Wheels, axle and a box, pulled by an animal.
nodes.l2: A cart multiplies how much one person and one animal can move by roughly an order of magnitude. That changes the economic radius of a settlement: how far fields can be from the village, how far grain can travel before the cost of moving it exceeds its value.
nodes.l3: Wagon burials, ceramic models, cart ruts and depictions in art document form and use. Draught-animal skeletons show pathologies from pulling loads, which independently confirms traction.
nodes.ev: Wagon burials; ceramic models; draught-animal pathology

nodes.l1: Trading distance for force — moving a heavy thing a short way by moving a light thing a long way.
nodes.l2: This is the central idea of pre-industrial engineering. Levers, pulleys, screws, wedges and inclined planes all do the same trick, and once the principle is stated abstractly it can be applied to any of them. It is also an early example of a general law being extracted from a set of specific tricks.
nodes.l3: Archimedes gave the law of the lever a formal treatment in the third century BCE, and his works on statics survive through later copies. The practical techniques are far older and visible in construction evidence.
nodes.ev: Archimedean statics; construction evidence; surviving machines

nodes.l1: A grooved wheel that redirects a rope — and, in sets, multiplies force.
nodes.l2: A single pulley only changes direction, which is already useful because pulling down is easier than lifting up. Several in a block-and-tackle divide the required force by the number of supporting rope lengths. This is how ancient construction lifted blocks that no crowd could carry.
nodes.l3: Pulley blocks survive from classical contexts, and crane bases and lifting-boss cuttings on stone blocks show where hoists were anchored. Roman treatises describe the machines directly.
nodes.ev: Surviving pulley blocks; lifting bosses; ancient engineering texts

nodes.l1: A rigid bar and a pivot. The simplest machine there is.
nodes.l2: A lever converts a small force over a long distance into a large force over a short one, and it requires nothing but a stick and a rock. It is almost certainly the oldest machine humans used, and it is still inside most mechanisms — every pair of scissors, every crank, every bone-and-muscle joint in your arm.
nodes.l3: Levering is inferred from what was moved rather than from surviving levers, since a wooden pole leaves no trace. Prying marks on megalithic stone and the geometry of construction sites indicate the technique.
nodes.ev: Prying marks on megaliths; construction geometry; later texts

nodes.l1: Toothed wheels that mesh, transmitting rotation at a chosen ratio.
nodes.l2: Gears make rotation programmable. A chosen tooth ratio converts speed into torque or the reverse, exactly and repeatably, and a train of gears can compute a ratio far too awkward to arrange any other way. Everything from clocks to gearboxes to differential drives is a consequence.
nodes.l3: The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a Greek shipwreck and dated to roughly the second century BCE, contains dozens of precisely cut bronze gears used to model astronomical cycles. Imaging by X-ray tomography reconstructed the gear train without dismantling it.
nodes.ev: Antikythera mechanism; X-ray tomography; ancient gear finds

nodes.l1: Parts arranged so that motion in one produces determined motion in another.
nodes.l2: A mechanism embodies a rule in metal. Given the input, the output is fixed by geometry — no decision, no supervision. This is the beginning of automation as a concept: behaviour built into a physical arrangement, and the direct ancestor of the idea that a machine can execute a procedure.
nodes.l3: Surviving devices, ancient engineering treatises such as those of Hero of Alexandria, and later medieval clockwork document the tradition. Tomographic imaging recovers internal arrangements from corroded objects.
nodes.ev: Surviving devices; ancient engineering texts; tomographic imaging

nodes.date: Practice is ancient; formal discipline from the 1700s
nodes.l1: Designing something to work before it exists, and knowing why it will.
nodes.l2: Engineering is the point where building stops being craft tradition and becomes calculation. You can predict whether a beam will hold, size it deliberately, and justify the number. That lets structures be built that nobody has attempted before, which craft tradition alone cannot do because tradition only encodes what has already worked.
