nodes.l3: The shift is visible in the documents: from pattern books and rules of thumb, to engineering drawings with dimensions and tolerances, to calculated load analyses. Professional societies and formal training appear alongside.
nodes.ev: Engineering drawings; calculated load analyses; professional records

nodes.l1: The systems everything else runs on, noticed mainly when they fail.
nodes.l2: Water supply, drainage, roads, ports, power and networks share a shape: enormous fixed cost, long life, benefits spread across everyone, and no individual incentive to build them. That is why infrastructure is almost always collective — and why its condition is one of the more reliable indicators of a society's capacity.
nodes.l3: Aqueducts, sewers, harbours and road networks survive as structures and are datable. Maintenance records — Roman water administration is documented in detail — show the ongoing cost that construction figures alone hide.
nodes.ev: Surviving aqueducts and sewers; maintenance records; port works

nodes.l1: Comparing a thing to an agreed standard and getting a number.
nodes.l2: Measurement converts judgement into fact. Without a shared unit, 'long enough' is an argument; with one, it is a check anyone can repeat. Trade needs it to prevent cheating, building needs it for parts that fit, and science needs it because a claim you cannot quantify is one you cannot test.
nodes.l3: Standard weights and measuring rods survive from Egypt, Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley — the Indus weights are notably consistent across hundreds of kilometres, which implies enforcement. Later, metrological standards are documented in law.
nodes.ev: Standard weights and rods; metrological legislation

nodes.l1: The mathematics of shape, distance and angle.
nodes.l2: Geometry began as land surveying — the word means 'earth measurement', and it was needed because the Nile flood erased field boundaries every year. Euclid then did something different: he showed that a large body of results could be derived from a handful of assumptions. That method, not the results, is geometry's real legacy.
nodes.l3: Practical geometry appears in Egyptian and Babylonian problem texts, including Pythagorean triples a millennium before Pythagoras. Euclid's Elements survives through a long manuscript tradition and remained a standard text for over two thousand years.
nodes.ev: Babylonian problem tablets; Rhind papyrus; Euclid's Elements

nodes.l1: Reasoning about abstract structure — and finding it describes the world.
nodes.l2: Mathematics starts as accounting and surveying, then does something strange: it detaches from application and studies structure for its own sake, and the results turn out to describe physical reality anyway. Conic sections were studied for centuries as pure geometry before planets were found to travel along them.
nodes.l3: The record runs from Babylonian and Egyptian problem texts through Greek proof, Indian and Islamic algebra and numerals, to modern formal systems — a continuous, cross-cultural manuscript and print tradition.
nodes.ev: Problem tablets; Greek proofs; algebraic and analytic manuscripts
nodes.caution: Mathematics is not a European invention. Major developments came from Mesopotamia, Egypt, India, China and the Islamic world.

nodes.l1: Understanding stored outside any living memory.
nodes.l2: Oral transmission is limited by how much a person can hold and how faithfully it survives each retelling. Written knowledge lifts both limits: it accumulates without decay and can be consulted by someone the author never met. This is what makes progress cumulative rather than cyclical.
nodes.l3: Library and archive collections — Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, the Egyptian medical papyri, the Chinese classics — survive in whole or in part. Manuscript traditions can be traced through copying errors, which reveal transmission lineages like a family tree.
nodes.ev: Library collections; manuscript stemmatics; medical and technical papyri

nodes.l1: Space represented on a surface you can hold.
nodes.l2: A map is an abstraction with a claim built in: it says what is worth showing and what is not. Reducing three dimensions to two lets a person reason about a territory larger than they can see, and compare places they have never simultaneously visited. It is also, unavoidably, an argument about the world.
nodes.l3: Babylonian clay maps, Egyptian mine plans and Chinese silk maps survive. Their distortions are informative: what is enlarged, centred or omitted tells you what mattered to the maker.
nodes.ev: Clay and papyrus maps; early survey plans
nodes.caution: Every map encodes the priorities of its maker. There is no neutral projection.

nodes.l1: Mapping as a measured discipline, with known distortions.
nodes.l2: Cartography is what happens when mapping meets mathematics. A sphere cannot be flattened without distortion — that is a theorem, not a technical shortcoming — so every projection sacrifices something, and the cartographer's job is choosing which. Accurate coordinates then require solving longitude, which took an accurate portable clock.
nodes.l3: Ptolemy's Geography sets out coordinates and projection methods in the second century CE. Later, national triangulation surveys and the eighteenth-century marine chronometer make position determination systematic.
nodes.ev: Ptolemy's Geography; triangulation surveys; chronometer records

nodes.l1: Looking carefully, on purpose, and writing down what you saw.
nodes.l2: The step that makes observation scientific is the record. A single impression is worth little; a series kept in a standard form for decades reveals patterns invisible in any one night. Babylonian sky records ran for centuries, and their value came entirely from that continuity.
nodes.l3: Astronomical diaries, ships' logs, meteorological registers and natural history notebooks constitute long observational series. Many are still used — historical logs feed modern climate reconstructions.
nodes.ev: Astronomical diaries; ships' logs; long observational series

nodes.l1: How light travels, bends and forms images.
nodes.l2: Optics is where geometry became physics. Once refraction is understood as a rule light obeys, lenses stop being curiosities and become designable instruments — and instruments extend the senses. Almost everything humans have learned about the very small and the very distant arrived through a lens.
nodes.l3: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics, around 1021, argues from controlled experiment that vision works by light entering the eye, overturning the prevailing theory. It is a landmark both in optics and in experimental method.
nodes.ev: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics; lens finds; later refraction studies

nodes.l1: Making small things large enough to see.
nodes.l2: Magnification revealed that there is an entire world below the threshold of the eye. Cells, microorganisms and crystal structure were not hidden by ignorance but by resolution — and the discovery that disease might be caused by things too small to see is one of the largest single changes in human survival.
nodes.l3: Hooke's Micrographia in 1665 and van Leeuwenhoek's letters to the Royal Society record and illustrate the first microscopic observations, with instruments that survive and have been replicated.
nodes.ev: Micrographia; van Leeuwenhoek's letters; surviving instruments

nodes.l1: An instrument that makes distant things resolvable.
nodes.l2: The telescope did something no argument could: it produced observations flatly incompatible with the accepted model of the cosmos. Moons orbiting Jupiter, phases of Venus, mountains on the Moon. The instrument settled a question that centuries of reasoning had not, which is a useful lesson about where knowledge comes from.
nodes.l3: Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius of 1610 publishes the observations with drawings. His instruments survive, and modern replicas confirm what was and was not visible through them.
nodes.ev: Sidereus Nuncius; surviving instruments; replica studies

nodes.l1: Arranging conditions deliberately to find out what happens.
nodes.l2: Observation waits for nature to show you something. Experiment makes it happen on your schedule, with everything held fixed except the one thing you changed — which is the only way to separate cause from coincidence. It is a deceptively simple idea that took a very long time to become standard practice.
nodes.l3: Ibn al-Haytham's controlled optical work is an early systematic case. Boyle, Hooke and their contemporaries formalised the reporting of apparatus and procedure in detail sufficient for others to repeat the work — which is where reproducibility as a norm begins.
nodes.ev: Early experimental reports; surviving apparatus; replication studies

nodes.l1: A procedure for finding out you were wrong as quickly as possible.
nodes.l2: The method's real content is not 'hypothesis, experiment, conclusion' — it is institutionalised self-doubt. Predictions must be specific enough to fail, results must be reported so others can repeat them, and conclusions stay provisional. It is slow and often ignored in practice, and it remains the most reliable knowledge-generating process anyone has found.
nodes.l3: The Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, from 1665, is the oldest continuously published scientific journal, and its early volumes show peer correspondence, replication attempts and public disputes over method.
nodes.ev: Early scientific journals; replication disputes; methodological treatises
nodes.caution: There is no single agreed 'scientific method'. Practice differs sharply between fields, and the textbook version is an idealisation.

nodes.date: ≈ 1687 CE onward as a mathematical science
nodes.l1: The rules matter and energy obey, written as mathematics.
nodes.l2: Newton's achievement was unification: the same law that governs a falling apple governs the Moon. Once physical law is mathematical, behaviour becomes calculable in advance — bridges, engines, orbits and circuits can all be designed rather than discovered by trial. Engineering as calculation begins here.
nodes.l3: The Principia of 1687 sets out the laws and derives consequences. Subsequent centuries add thermodynamics, electromagnetism, relativity and quantum mechanics, each documented by prediction-then-confirmation episodes that are unusually well recorded.
nodes.ev: Principia; predictive confirmations; experimental record

nodes.date: ≈ 1780s CE onward as a quantitative science
nodes.l1: What substances are made of, and what happens when they meet.
nodes.l2: Chemistry became a science when it started weighing things. Lavoisier's insistence on mass balance in closed systems killed the phlogiston theory and established conservation of mass, converting a craft tradition of recipes into a predictive discipline. Materials could then be designed rather than stumbled upon.
nodes.l3: Lavoisier's quantitative combustion experiments are documented with apparatus and figures. The periodic table's predictive successes — elements whose properties were forecast before discovery — are a well-recorded test of the framework.
nodes.ev: Lavoisier's quantitative experiments; periodic table predictions

nodes.l1: Trying to make sick people better — with very mixed results for most of history.
nodes.l2: Medicine is ancient; effective medicine is recent. For millennia treatment was as likely to harm as help, and the honest version of this story includes bloodletting and mercury. What changed was not compassion but method: controlled comparison, statistics, germ theory and the willingness to abandon a treatment that fails to outperform doing nothing.
nodes.l3: Egyptian and Mesopotamian medical texts document early practice. Lind's scurvy comparison in 1747 is an early controlled trial; nineteenth-century sanitation statistics and twentieth-century randomised trials establish the modern evidentiary standard.
nodes.ev: Ancient medical papyri; early controlled trials; mortality statistics
nodes.caution: Traditional does not mean effective. Most historical treatments did not work, and some were actively harmful.

nodes.l1: What the body is actually made of, established by looking inside it.
nodes.l2: Anatomy matters because you cannot fix a mechanism you have not seen. Vesalius's insistence on dissecting rather than deferring to Galen corrected errors that had stood for over a thousand years, and established a norm: check the authority against the object.
nodes.l3: Vesalius's De Humani Corporis Fabrica of 1543 pairs systematic dissection with detailed plates. Later imaging — X-ray, CT, MRI — extends the same project non-destructively.
nodes.ev: Anatomical atlases; dissection records; modern imaging

nodes.date: ≈ 1859 CE onward as a unified science
nodes.l1: The study of living things, unified by a single explanatory idea.
nodes.l2: Before evolution, biology was cataloguing. Descent with modification through natural selection explained why the catalogue has the shape it does — why species nest into groups, why vestigial structures exist, why the fossil sequence runs as it does. Genetics later supplied the mechanism Darwin lacked.
nodes.l3: The convergence is the strength: comparative anatomy, palaeontology, biogeography, embryology and molecular genetics were developed independently and agree on the same branching pattern. Directly observed evolution in fast-reproducing organisms adds real-time confirmation.
nodes.ev: Fossil sequences; comparative genomics; observed evolution
nodes.caution: Biological evolution has no goal and no direction toward complexity. It is differential survival and reproduction, not improvement toward a plan.

nodes.l1: Extracting reliable conclusions from unreliable individual observations.
nodes.l2: Statistics is how science handles noise. It supplies a way to say how strongly evidence supports a claim, and — as importantly — how easily a result could have arisen by chance. Every modern empirical field runs on it, and most of its famous failures are failures to apply it honestly.
nodes.l3: Graunt's analysis of London mortality bills in 1662 is an early demographic study. Later work on error distributions, sampling and significance testing built the formal apparatus, alongside a long-running and still-live debate about how it should be used.
nodes.ev: Early mortality analyses; sampling theory; trial methodology
nodes.caution: Statistical significance is not importance, and correlation is not causation. Both mistakes remain common in published work.

nodes.l1: Recorded observations, structured so they can be counted and compared.
nodes.l2: Data is not the same as knowledge, and the gap between them is where most errors live. What gets measured reflects who was doing the measuring and what they cared about; gaps in a dataset are rarely random. Data is enormously powerful and never neutral.
nodes.l3: Long-run datasets — censuses, price series, weather registers, astronomical catalogues — are themselves historical objects, and studying how they were collected is a discipline in its own right.
nodes.ev: Census and administrative series; scientific catalogues; archives
nodes.caution: Datasets carry the biases of their collection. Missing data is usually missing for a reason.

nodes.l1: People who check each other's work, at a distance, over generations.
nodes.l2: Science is a social institution before it is a method. Its reliability comes from many independent people trying to find fault in a claim — through journals, replication, correspondence and open dispute. An isolated genius has no way to catch their own systematic errors; a community does, imperfectly.
nodes.l3: Learned societies, their journals and their correspondence networks are documented from the seventeenth century onward. The Republic of Letters — a cross-border scholarly correspondence network — is reconstructable from surviving letters.
nodes.ev: Learned society records; journal archives; correspondence networks

nodes.l1: A river turning a wheel, continuously, for free.
nodes.l2: Water power was the first energy source that worked while nobody watched it. A watermill delivers far more sustained power than muscle, day and night, and its geography dictated where industry could be — early factories clustered along fast rivers because that was where the power was.
nodes.l3: Mill sites, wheel pits, leats and dam structures survive and are datable. Medieval surveys such as Domesday count mills in the thousands, giving a quantitative picture of the installed base.
nodes.ev: Mill structures and wheel pits; medieval mill surveys

nodes.l1: Extracting work from moving air.
nodes.l2: Wind works where water does not — on flat, dry land with no fall. Its drawback is intermittency, the same problem modern renewables face, and the historical answer was the same one used now: store the output rather than the wind, by grinding ahead or pumping water uphill.
nodes.l3: Windmill structures survive across Persia, Europe and China, with regional designs — vertical-axis in Persia, horizontal-axis post mills in Europe. Estate records document construction, output and repair.
nodes.ev: Surviving mills; estate and manorial records

nodes.l1: Rotary motion distributed to wherever the work is.
nodes.l2: Having power is not enough; it has to reach the machine. Line shafting, belts and gearing let one prime mover drive dozens of machines across a building — and that requirement is exactly why early factories are long, narrow and multi-storey. The building is shaped by the transmission system.
nodes.l3: Mill interiors preserve shafting, belt routes and machine mountings. Insurance plans and engineering drawings record transmission layouts in detail.
nodes.ev: Surviving shafting and mountings; mill plans; engineering drawings

nodes.date: Used for millennia; industrial from the 1700s
nodes.l1: Buried carbon from ancient forests, burning far hotter than wood.
nodes.l2: Coal breaks a hard constraint. Wood and charcoal are limited by how fast forests grow, and by the eighteenth century Britain was running out. Coal is a stock rather than a flow — millions of years of stored sunlight available at once — and access to it is what made sustained industrial growth possible at all.
nodes.l3: Production statistics, mine records and geological surveys document the transition. Coal use also leaves an environmental record in soot layers, ice cores and lake sediments.
nodes.ev: Mine and production records; geological survey; pollution proxies
nodes.caution: Coal removed an energy ceiling and began the sustained rise in atmospheric CO₂ that continues today. Both consequences belong in the same sentence.

nodes.l1: Water turned to vapour, expanding to roughly 1,700 times its liquid volume.
nodes.l2: That expansion is the useful part: heat becomes pressure, and pressure becomes motion. Hero of Alexandria built a steam-spun toy in the first century CE and nothing followed, because there was no need for concentrated power and no metallurgy to contain pressure. Technology needs a problem and a supply chain, not just an idea.
nodes.l3: Hero's aeolipile is described in surviving texts. Practical steam appears with Savery's and Newcomen's engines, documented in patents, engine records and surviving hardware.
nodes.ev: Ancient descriptions; engine patents; surviving engines
nodes.caution: The steam toy of antiquity did not lead to the steam engine. Ideas without an economic need and a materials base go nowhere.

nodes.l1: Burning fuel to produce mechanical work, anywhere you want it.
nodes.l2: The steam engine broke the tie between power and place. Water power required a river; steam required only fuel, so factories could be sited by labour and transport instead of geography. Newcomen's engine of 1712 pumped water out of mines — including coal mines, so the engine fed its own fuel supply. Watt's separate condenser then cut coal consumption enough to make it viable far beyond mining.
nodes.l3: Newcomen and Watt engines survive, alongside patents, engine-house records and fuel-consumption figures that quantify the efficiency improvement directly.
nodes.ev: Surviving engines; patents; documented fuel consumption

nodes.l1: Production concentrated under one roof, on someone else's schedule.
nodes.l2: The factory's innovation is organisational as much as mechanical. Bringing workers to a central power source imposed clock discipline, supervision and a fixed working day on people who had previously worked to task and season. The social conflict that followed — over hours, child labour, safety — shaped modern labour law.
nodes.l3: Factory buildings survive. Wage books, factory inspection reports and parliamentary inquiries document conditions in detail, including testimony from workers.
nodes.ev: Surviving mills; wage books; factory inspectorate reports
nodes.caution: Early factory conditions were severe, including widespread child labour. Output figures and human cost are both part of the record.

nodes.l1: An economy reorganised around machine production and fossil energy.
nodes.l2: Industrialisation ended the Malthusian pattern in which output growth was cancelled by population growth. For the first time, output per person rose sustainably — and it did so unevenly, with enormous regional divergence, severe early conditions, and environmental consequences that were invisible at the time and are not now.
nodes.l3: Long-run GDP, wage, energy and output series document the transition quantitatively. Health and mortality data give the human picture, which lags the economic one by decades.
nodes.ev: Long-run economic series; energy statistics; mortality data

nodes.l1: Machines that make machine parts more accurately than hands can.
nodes.l2: This is the quiet bottleneck of the whole industrial era. Watt's engine needed a cylinder bored accurately enough to hold steam, and it was Wilkinson's boring machine that made that possible. Precision compounds: better tools make better tools, and the achievable tolerance of an entire economy ratchets upward.
nodes.l3: Surviving lathes, boring mills and planers, together with their documented tolerances, track the improvement. Gauge blocks and standards make the precision claims checkable.
nodes.ev: Surviving machine tools; documented tolerances; gauge standards

nodes.l1: Components made alike enough that any one fits any assembly.
nodes.l2: Interchangeability sounds mundane and changes everything. It makes assembly unskilled, repair a matter of replacement rather than refitting, and supply chains possible across companies and continents. It requires tolerances, gauges and inspection — and it is the precondition for mass production.
nodes.l3: Armoury records and public demonstrations of interchangeability, together with the development of gauging systems and later national standards bodies, document the shift.
nodes.ev: Armoury records; gauge systems; national standards

nodes.l1: Making enormous numbers of the same thing very cheaply.
nodes.l2: The moving assembly line brings work to the worker and divides it into steps of a few seconds each. Unit cost collapses; so does the variety on offer and the skill content of the job. Mass production is why manufactured goods became affordable to the people making them — and why so much twentieth-century labour conflict is about the pace of the line.
nodes.l3: Production figures, time-and-motion studies and factory records document both the output gains and the labour effects. Price series show the resulting collapse in consumer cost.
nodes.ev: Production and price series; time-and-motion records

nodes.l1: Guided steel track that lets a small force move a huge load.
nodes.l2: Steel wheel on steel rail has extraordinarily low rolling resistance — an order of magnitude less than a wheel on a road. That is the physics behind the railway's economics. Its social effect was time itself: railways forced the abolition of local solar time and the adoption of standard time zones, because a timetable cannot work otherwise.
nodes.l3: Route maps, timetables, company records and surviving infrastructure document the network's growth. The adoption of standard time is recorded in legislation and railway company rulebooks.
nodes.ev: Company records; timetables; standard-time legislation

nodes.l1: A steam engine that carries its own fuel and moves itself.
nodes.l2: Making the engine mobile required a high-pressure boiler light enough to carry — which meant better iron, better boilermaking and accepting the risk of explosion. Once achieved, land transport ceased to depend on animal muscle for the first time in history.
nodes.l3: Surviving locomotives, trial records such as the Rainhill trials of 1829, and engineering drawings document performance and development.
nodes.ev: Surviving locomotives; trial records; engineering drawings

nodes.date: ≈ 1800 CE onward as a usable phenomenon
nodes.l1: Charge in motion — the most flexible form of energy yet found.
nodes.l2: Electricity's advantage is convertibility. It moves along a wire with modest loss and turns into motion, heat, light, sound or computation at the far end. That generality is why it became the universal carrier: almost any energy source can be converted into it, and it into almost any use.
nodes.l3: Volta's pile of 1800 provided the first steady current, making systematic study possible. Faraday's induction experiments of 1831 and Maxwell's equations of the 1860s established the theory that made design possible.
nodes.ev: Volta's pile; Faraday's notebooks; Maxwell's equations

nodes.l1: Turning a shaft to make current — at central stations, for everyone.
nodes.l2: Generation plus a grid separates where energy is produced from where it is used. A factory no longer needs its own prime mover, a home can have light without a flame, and the entire spatial logic of industry changes. The grid is arguably the largest machine ever built, and it must balance supply and demand continuously.
nodes.l3: Pearl Street Station in 1882 and the subsequent alternating-current systems are documented in company records, patents and surviving plant. Electrification rates are tracked in national statistics.
nodes.ev: Station records; patents; electrification statistics

nodes.l1: Current in, rotation out. The generator run backwards.
nodes.l2: The motor killed line shafting. Instead of one central engine driving every machine through belts, each machine got its own motor — so factory layout could follow the work rather than the drive shaft, and small motors could go into tools, appliances and vehicles. Most machines you touch daily contain one.
nodes.l3: Early motors survive, and patents plus factory reorganisation records document the transition from shafting to unit drive, including the productivity gains that followed with a decades-long lag.
nodes.ev: Surviving motors; patents; factory layout records

nodes.l1: Light without fire.
nodes.l2: Artificial light is one of the clearest cases of long-run technological progress: the labour cost of an hour of light has fallen by orders of magnitude since candles. That made the evening usable for reading and work, extended factory shifts, and changed sleep patterns across whole populations.
nodes.l3: The Smithsonian's Lighting A Revolution documents the invention process, including the many parallel workers usually omitted from the Edison story. Long-run price-of-light series quantify the change.
nodes.ev: Invention records and surviving lamps; price-of-light series
nodes.caution: Electric light was not one inventor's work. Many researchers across several countries contributed, and the popular single-inventor account is misleading.

nodes.l1: Messages travelling faster than any messenger.
nodes.l2: This is the break. For all of prior history, information moved at the speed of a horse, a ship or a runner — so distant events were always old news. The telegraph severs message from messenger, and the consequences are immediate: financial markets synchronise, empires tighten, news becomes same-day, and standard time becomes necessary.
nodes.l3: Telegraph company records, message traffic volumes, cable-laying logs and surviving apparatus document the network. Price convergence between distant markets is measurable in commodity series and is a clean economic signature.
nodes.ev: Company and traffic records; cable logs; market price convergence

nodes.l1: The voice itself, carried down a wire.
nodes.l2: The telegraph needed an operator and a code; the telephone needed neither, which made distant communication available to anyone who could speak. It also made it conversational rather than transactional — real-time back-and-forth rather than dispatch and reply — and that shifted what long-distance contact was for.
nodes.l3: Patents, exchange records and subscriber statistics document adoption, alongside surviving instruments. Switchboard and later automatic exchange technology is documented in engineering records.
nodes.ev: Patents; exchange and subscriber records; surviving instruments

nodes.l1: A society where most people work for wages and live in cities.
nodes.l2: Within a few generations the majority occupation shifted from farming to wage work, and the majority residence from countryside to city. That reorganised family structure, education, politics and identity. It also produced mass schooling, public health systems and organised labour — institutions built to handle a way of living that had no precedent.
nodes.l3: Census occupational data, urbanisation series and long-run health statistics document the transition across many countries, with sharply different timing that itself is informative.
nodes.ev: Census occupation data; urbanisation series; public health statistics

nodes.l1: Fixing an image made by light, without anyone drawing it.
nodes.l2: Before photography, every image was filtered through a human hand and a human choice. A photograph is made by the light itself, which gave it an authority no painting had — and which turned out to be partly an illusion, since framing, timing and processing are all choices. Still, it changed evidence, memory, news and identity.
nodes.l3: Surviving early plates, patents and process manuals document the chemistry. The first photographs are datable and their processes reproducible; modern practitioners still make daguerreotypes with period methods.
nodes.ev: Surviving plates; process patents; reproduction of historic processes
nodes.caution: A photograph is not a neutral record. Framing, exposure and processing are all editorial choices, long before digital manipulation existed.

nodes.l1: Burning fuel inside the cylinder instead of under a boiler.
nodes.l2: Moving combustion inside removes the boiler, the water and most of the mass. The result is far more power per kilogram, which is exactly what a vehicle needs and what a steam engine could not deliver. Every consequence of personal mobility and powered flight follows from that ratio.
nodes.l3: Otto's four-stroke cycle of 1876 is documented in patents and surviving engines. Thermodynamic analysis explains the efficiency ceiling, and it matches measured performance.
nodes.ev: Otto-cycle patents; surviving engines; thermodynamic analysis

nodes.l1: Personal transport that goes where there is no track and no timetable.
nodes.l2: The car offers door-to-door travel on individual schedule, and people have consistently valued that enough to accept its costs. Those costs are substantial and were mostly unforeseen: cities rebuilt around parking and roads, a large annual toll of deaths, and a major share of global emissions.
nodes.l3: Production and registration statistics, road-network data, and casualty and emissions series document both the adoption and its consequences over more than a century.
nodes.ev: Production and registration statistics; casualty and emissions data
nodes.caution: Mass motorisation reshaped cities and carries large ongoing costs in casualties and emissions. Convenience and cost belong in the same account.

nodes.l1: Heavier-than-air machines that stay up on purpose.
nodes.l2: The Wrights' decisive contribution was not lift — that was understood — but control. They solved three-axis control, which is what turns a glider into an aircraft you can fly deliberately. They also built a wind tunnel and generated their own aerodynamic data because the published tables were wrong.
nodes.l3: The Wright Flyer is held by the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum. The brothers' notebooks, wind-tunnel data, patents and photographs of the 1903 flights survive and are well studied.
nodes.ev: Wright Flyer; notebooks and wind-tunnel data; 1903 photographs

nodes.l1: Still images shown fast enough that the eye reads motion.
nodes.l2: Cinema exploits a limitation of human perception and builds an art form on it. More than that, it invented a grammar — cut, close-up, cross-cut, montage — for assembling time so that an audience constructs a story from fragments. Every screen medium since, video games included, inherited that vocabulary.
nodes.l3: Surviving films, projection equipment, patents and studio records document the technology and its language. Early films are dated and their techniques directly analysable frame by frame.
nodes.ev: Surviving films and equipment; patents; studio records

nodes.l1: A glass bulb that controls electrons — the first electronic component.
nodes.l2: The vacuum tube can amplify a weak signal and switch on and off with no moving parts, which is exactly what radio, long-distance telephony and early computers required. It was also hot, fragile, power-hungry and prone to failure — the ENIAC's tubes failed often enough that finding the dead one was a routine task.
nodes.l3: Surviving tubes and equipment, patents, and the maintenance logs of early computers document both capability and failure rate. The Computer History Museum holds machines and components.
nodes.ev: Surviving tubes and machines; patents; maintenance logs

nodes.l1: Using small currents to control other currents.
nodes.l2: Electrical engineering moves power; electronics moves information. Once a device can amplify and switch, signals can be processed rather than merely transmitted — and switching is what makes logic physically possible. Every computer is, at bottom, a very large arrangement of switches.
nodes.l3: Component development, circuit theory and the standards that made mass-produced electronics possible are documented in patents, engineering literature and IEEE milestone records.
nodes.ev: Patents; circuit theory literature; engineering standards

nodes.l1: Communication with no wire between the ends.
nodes.l2: Radio removes the last physical constraint on communication. It reaches ships at sea, aircraft, remote regions and — crucially — everyone at once, which made mass broadcasting possible and gave the twentieth century its characteristic political instrument. Every wireless technology since is a descendant.
nodes.l3: Maxwell predicted electromagnetic waves; Hertz demonstrated them; Marconi and others engineered practical transmission. Patents, the maritime distress record and broadcasting archives document the development.
nodes.ev: Hertz's experiments; patents; maritime and broadcast records

nodes.l1: A material that conducts electricity only when you tell it to.
nodes.l2: Semiconductors sit between conductor and insulator, and adding controlled trace impurities — doping — tunes exactly how they behave. That controllability is the whole basis of modern electronics: it lets a switch be built with no moving parts, at a scale limited only by how precisely the material can be patterned.
nodes.l3: Semiconductor physics is documented in the research literature and in the Nobel citation for the transistor. Purity and doping requirements are recorded in process specifications; the achieved purity of silicon is among the highest of any bulk material made.
nodes.ev: Semiconductor physics literature; process specifications

nodes.l1: A switch with no moving parts, and it can be made almost arbitrarily small.
nodes.l2: The transistor does what the vacuum tube did, using a fraction of the power, in a fraction of the space, with far greater reliability. Crucially, it gets better as it gets smaller — which is the property that made decades of exponential improvement possible. It is arguably the most-manufactured object in human history.
nodes.l3: The 1947 Bell Labs work by Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley was recognised with the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics 'for their researches on semiconductors and their discovery of the transistor effect'. Laboratory notebooks and the original devices survive.
nodes.ev: Bell Labs notebooks; original devices; Nobel Prize record

nodes.l1: Many components made together on one piece of material, wired in place.
nodes.l2: The problem the IC solved was not size but connections — a circuit with thousands of separately soldered parts is unbuildable and unreliable. Fabricating components and their wiring simultaneously on one substrate removes the assembly step entirely, and the cost per component then falls as the count rises. That inversion is what makes cheap computing possible.
nodes.l3: Kilby's and Noyce's devices, patents and fabrication records are held and documented by the Computer History Museum. Transistor-count series over decades quantify the scaling directly.
nodes.ev: Original devices and patents; transistor-count series

nodes.l1: A machine that follows a stored list of instructions, whatever they say.
nodes.l2: Earlier machines did one thing. The decisive idea — a machine holding its instructions in the same memory as its data — makes one machine capable of any computable task, including modifying its own program. Generality is the whole point: the hardware stops determining the application.
nodes.l3: Early machines and their documentation survive: Colossus, ENIAC, the Manchester Baby, EDSAC. Turing's 1936 paper set out the theoretical model before the machines existed, and it still describes what they can and cannot do.
nodes.ev: Surviving early machines; design reports; Turing's 1936 paper
nodes.caution: There is no single inventor of the computer. Several machines in Britain, the United States and Germany have competing claims depending on which criteria are used.

nodes.l1: Writing the instructions the machine will follow.
nodes.l2: Programming is where computing stops being electrical engineering and becomes something closer to writing. Ada Lovelace's notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine, published in 1843, argued that such a machine could operate on symbols generally rather than only on numbers — the idea that the machine is not merely a calculator.
nodes.l3: Lovelace's published notes survive, as do early program listings, punched cards and machine documentation. Programming's history includes the substantial and long-underacknowledged contribution of women, documented in institutional records.
nodes.ev: Lovelace's 1843 notes; early program listings; punched cards

nodes.l1: Fast storage the processor can reach immediately.
nodes.l2: A computer's speed is limited as much by how fast it can reach data as by how fast it can calculate. That gap has widened for decades, which is why modern machines are built as layered hierarchies of caches. Much of the art of fast software is really the art of arranging data so the memory system cooperates.
nodes.l3: Magnetic core memory planes, delay lines and later semiconductor memory survive in museum collections, alongside the engineering documentation and access-time specifications that make the hierarchy visible.
nodes.ev: Surviving memory hardware; access-time specifications

nodes.l1: Keeping data when the power goes off.
nodes.l2: Persistent storage is what lets computers accumulate rather than merely calculate. Cost per byte has fallen by something like eight orders of magnitude since the 1950s, and that decline — more than processor speed — is what made it reasonable to keep everything instead of deciding what to discard.
nodes.l3: IBM's RAMAC of 1956, the first hard disk drive, is documented and preserved. Long-run cost-per-byte series quantify the decline across tape, disk and solid-state generations.
nodes.ev: RAMAC and successor drives; cost-per-byte series

nodes.date: ≈ 1950s CE onward as a distinct thing
nodes.l1: The part of the machine that has no physical existence.
nodes.l2: Software separated from hardware and became an industry, an art and a permanent maintenance problem. Its distinguishing economics: essentially zero cost to copy, very high cost to build correctly, and a defect rate that no amount of care eliminates. Most large software failures are failures of complexity management, not of coding.
nodes.l3: Source code, version histories, defect databases and post-mortem reports of major failures are extensively documented. Historic source is preserved by museums and archives, including operating systems and language compilers.
nodes.ev: Preserved source code; version histories; failure post-mortems

nodes.l1: A whole processor on a single chip.
nodes.l2: Putting the processor on one inexpensive component turned computing from an institutional asset into a part you could design into anything — a till, a car, a washing machine, a watch, a phone. Far more microprocessors are sold into embedded uses than into anything recognisable as a computer.
nodes.l3: The Intel 4004 of 1971 and its successors are preserved and documented, with die photographs, datasheets and production figures. Transistor-count and price series track the trajectory.
nodes.ev: Preserved chips and datasheets; die photographs; production figures

nodes.l1: A computer owned by a person rather than an institution.
nodes.l2: The shift is about control as much as cost. When the machine belongs to you, you decide what it runs, and a hobbyist can write and distribute software without asking anyone. That is the precondition for most of the software culture, and most of the games, that followed.
nodes.l3: Machines, manuals, user-group newsletters and software libraries from the period are preserved. Sales figures and household penetration statistics document adoption.
nodes.ev: Preserved machines and software; user-group publications; sales data

nodes.l1: Making pictures by calculating them.
nodes.l2: Graphics made computers usable by people who are not programmers. Sutherland's Sketchpad in 1963 demonstrated direct manipulation — draw on the screen, the machine responds — and that idea leads to every graphical interface since. It also means images can be generated from a model rather than captured from the world.
nodes.l3: Sketchpad is documented in Sutherland's thesis and in film of the system running. The Computer History Museum's graphics and games timeline records the subsequent development in detail.
nodes.ev: Sketchpad thesis and film; museum timeline; early systems

nodes.l1: Sound, image and text reduced to numbers.
nodes.l2: Once media is numbers, copying is exact and free, editing is non-destructive, and transmission is just data. Every business model built on the scarcity of physical copies broke, and the resulting fights over copyright, distribution and value are still running four decades later.
nodes.l3: Format specifications, compression standards and the recorded history of the industries affected — music, film, publishing — document the transition, alongside revenue and distribution statistics.
nodes.ev: Format and compression standards; industry revenue series

nodes.l1: Machines that can talk to each other.
nodes.l2: Connecting computers changes what a computer is for. Alone it computes; connected it communicates, and the communication turns out to matter more. Packet switching — chopping messages into pieces routed independently — was the key idea, and it is what makes a network survive damage and share capacity efficiently.
nodes.l3: ARPANET's design documents, the Requests for Comments series and the original hardware are preserved. The RFC archive is a continuous public record of how the protocols were argued out.
nodes.ev: ARPANET documentation; RFC series; preserved hardware

nodes.l1: A network of networks that no one owns or controls.
nodes.l2: The internet's design choice was to keep the network simple and push intelligence to the edges. That is why it could be extended by anyone without permission — the network does not need to know what your application does. Nearly everything unexpected that happened on it is a consequence of that decision.
nodes.l3: The design rationale is documented by its architects in 'A Brief History of the Internet', and the entire protocol development is public in the RFC series. Growth is tracked by host counts and adoption statistics.
nodes.ev: Architects' published history; RFC series; adoption statistics

nodes.l1: Documents that link to each other across the whole network.
nodes.l2: The web is an application running on the internet, not the internet itself — a distinction worth keeping. Its contribution was making the network usable by people rather than by systems administrators: a naming scheme, a markup language and a protocol, given away rather than licensed.
nodes.l3: Berners-Lee's 1989 proposal at CERN survives, as do the first server and browser. CERN has reconstructed the original browser, and the early specifications are public.
nodes.ev: 1989 CERN proposal; first server and browser; specifications

nodes.l1: The program through which most people experience the network.
nodes.l2: The browser started as a document viewer and became the most widely used application platform on Earth. Adding images, then scripting, then graphics and audio turned a page reader into a runtime — which is why so much software now ships as a website rather than as a program you install.
nodes.l3: Early browsers are preserved and runnable, and the standards that define browser behaviour are public. Market share and capability timelines document the platform's expansion.
nodes.ev: Preserved browsers; public web standards; market share data

nodes.l1: Talking to anyone, anywhere, essentially free.
nodes.l2: The cost of sending a message fell effectively to zero, and volume rose accordingly. The consequences cut both ways: contact maintained across any distance, and also attention markets, information cascades and harassment at scale. The technology is the same in both cases; the difference is in the incentives layered on top.
nodes.l3: Message-volume statistics, platform adoption data and a large research literature on social effects document the change. Early email and messaging systems are preserved.
nodes.ev: Traffic and adoption statistics; preserved early systems
nodes.caution: Effects on attention, polarisation and wellbeing are actively researched and contested. Strong claims in either direction outrun the evidence.

nodes.l1: A networked computer that is always with you.
nodes.l2: The smartphone folds together the computer, the camera, the map, the telephone, the music player and the payment card, and the important part is that it is always on and always connected. For a majority of people alive today it is the primary computer, and for many it was the first.
nodes.l3: Shipment and penetration statistics, teardown analyses of components, and connectivity data document adoption. Our World in Data tracks mobile subscription and internet access rates globally.
nodes.ev: Shipment and penetration statistics; component teardowns

nodes.l1: Someone else's computers, rented by the minute.
nodes.l2: The cloud turns capital expenditure into operating expenditure, which lets a small team command computing capacity that once required a corporation. That is genuinely democratising and it is also concentrating: a handful of providers now host a large share of the world's services, and their outages are everyone's outages.
nodes.l3: Provider capacity disclosures, energy consumption reporting for data centres, and market concentration figures document scale. Outage post-mortems are public and show dependency structure.
nodes.ev: Provider disclosures; data-centre energy reporting; outage records

nodes.l1: Systems that perform tasks previously thought to require a mind.
nodes.l2: The field's history is a cycle of overpromise and retrenchment. What changed in the 2010s was not a conceptual breakthrough so much as scale: much more data, much more compute, and learned representations replacing hand-written rules. What these systems actually understand — if that word applies — remains genuinely unsettled.
nodes.l3: Training-compute series, benchmark results and published model papers document capability growth. Our World in Data tracks compute used in notable AI systems over decades, showing an extremely steep curve.
nodes.ev: Training-compute series; benchmark results; published research
nodes.caution: Claims about machine understanding, reasoning and consciousness are contested and often overstated in both directions. Benchmark performance is not the same as competence.

nodes.date: Games are ancient; the discipline is recent
nodes.l1: Designing rules that make voluntary difficulty enjoyable.
nodes.l2: Games long predate computers — the Royal Game of Ur is roughly 4,500 years old and its rules have been partially reconstructed from a cuneiform tablet. What game design adds is deliberate authorship of a system whose whole purpose is to be interesting to inhabit: rules, feedback, difficulty curve, and meaningful choice.
nodes.l3: Ancient board games survive with boards, pieces and, occasionally, written rules. Modern design is documented in design documents, playtest records and postmortems published by developers.
nodes.ev: Ancient board games and rule tablets; design documents; playtest records

nodes.l1: A computed world that responds to what you do.
nodes.l2: Every earlier medium presents; a game responds. That difference makes the audience a participant whose choices change what happens, which is why games can teach systems in a way film and text cannot — you learn a rule by living inside it rather than being told it.
nodes.l3: Spacewar!, written in 1962 on a PDP-1, is preserved and still runs on restored hardware at the Computer History Museum. Earlier experiments such as Tennis for Two are documented, and priority claims are argued in the literature.
nodes.ev: Spacewar! on restored PDP-1; preserved systems; industry records

nodes.l1: A computer built for one purpose, sold at a price that assumes you will buy games.
nodes.l2: Fixed hardware is a gift to developers: every unit is identical, so a game can be optimised to the exact machine in a way PC software never can. That is why consoles historically punched above their raw specifications, and why late-generation games look so much better than launch titles on identical hardware.
nodes.l3: Consoles, development kits and technical documentation are preserved. Sales figures and the recorded history of the 1983 market crash document the industry's volatility.
nodes.ev: Preserved consoles and dev kits; technical documentation; sales data

nodes.l1: Building a model in three dimensions and computing the view.
nodes.l2: A 3D scene stores geometry, not pictures — so the camera can be anywhere, and the image is produced on demand. That is what makes a navigable space possible rather than a set of prepared views, and it is the technical precondition for every open world in this graph.
nodes.l3: Foundational algorithms — hidden surface removal, Gouraud and Phong shading, texture mapping, Z-buffering — are documented in published papers, most from the University of Utah group in the 1970s, and are still in use.
nodes.ev: Published rendering algorithms; early systems; museum collections

nodes.l1: Drawing a complete image in about sixteen milliseconds, sixty times a second.
nodes.l2: Real-time rendering is engineering under a hard deadline. A film frame can take hours; a game frame cannot take longer than the budget, ever, or the illusion breaks. Almost every technique in real-time graphics is an approximation chosen because it looks close enough and finishes in time.
nodes.l3: GPU architectures, graphics APIs and the published research on real-time approximation techniques document the field. Frame-time profiling makes the budget directly measurable.
nodes.ev: GPU architecture documentation; graphics APIs; published techniques

nodes.l1: Software that makes objects fall, collide and topple plausibly.
nodes.l2: A physics engine is not physics. It is a set of approximations tuned to look right and run fast, and it will happily violate conservation laws if that produces a better result. This is a useful thing to know about simulation generally: fidelity is chosen against cost, and 'realistic' usually means 'convincing'.
nodes.l3: Engine source, technical papers on collision detection and constraint solvers, and developer documentation describe the methods and their known failure modes explicitly.
nodes.ev: Engine source and documentation; published simulation methods
nodes.caution: Game physics is deliberately inaccurate. It optimises for plausibility and speed, not for correctness.

nodes.l1: Motion authored frame by frame, or generated between keys.
nodes.l2: Animation is the study of how movement communicates. The principles worked out by hand animators — anticipation, follow-through, timing, weight — transferred directly to computer animation, because they describe perception rather than technique. A character reads as alive because of timing, not polygon count.
nodes.l3: Animation principles are documented in the practitioner literature and remain standard teaching. Digital animation techniques — skeletal rigging, blending, inverse kinematics — are described in published research and tool documentation.
nodes.ev: Practitioner literature; published animation research; production records

nodes.l1: Recording a real performance and driving a digital character with it.
nodes.l2: Motion capture solves the problem that human observers are extremely good at spotting wrong human movement. Recording an actual performer gets the micro-timing right in a way hand animation struggles to. It also relocates authorship: the performance is the actor's, and the industry took a while to acknowledge that.
nodes.l3: Capture systems, calibration methods and production pipelines are documented technically. Its ancestor, rotoscoping — tracing filmed footage — dates to the 1910s and is documented in patents.
nodes.ev: Capture system documentation; production pipelines; rotoscope patents

nodes.l1: Reusable machinery so each game does not rebuild everything from nothing.
nodes.l2: Separating engine from content is the industrial move that made large games feasible. It also changed who can make games: engines that are free to start with put a professional toolchain in the hands of individuals, which is why so much of the interesting work now comes from very small teams.
nodes.l3: Engine architecture is documented in technical literature and in released source for several historically important engines. Licensing records and credits track adoption across the industry.
nodes.ev: Released engine source; architecture literature; licensing records

nodes.l1: Content generated by rules instead of placed by hand.
nodes.l2: Procedural generation trades authored detail for scale: a rule that makes plausible terrain can fill a continent that no team could build by hand. The permanent tension is that generated content is abundant and rarely memorable, so the strongest uses combine generated bulk with hand-authored landmarks.
nodes.l3: Techniques such as Perlin noise, L-systems and wave function collapse are published with implementations. Early examples — Elite fitting a galaxy into a few kilobytes by generating it from a seed — are preserved and analysed.
nodes.ev: Published algorithms; preserved early titles; technical postmortems

nodes.l1: An urban space you can move through that does not exist.
nodes.l2: A convincing virtual city needs more than geometry: traffic that flows, pedestrians with somewhere to be, lighting that changes, sound that comes from the right place. It is a simulation of urban life at just enough depth to survive being looked at, and the interesting engineering is deciding what can be faked.
nodes.l3: Development postmortems, technical talks and published research on crowd and traffic simulation document the methods. Real-world reference material — photography, survey data and increasingly lidar — is used in production.
nodes.ev: Developer technical talks; crowd and traffic simulation research

nodes.l1: A space you can go anywhere in, in any order.
nodes.l2: Open-world design gives up control of sequence, which means the designer can no longer guarantee what the player has seen. Everything must work from any direction, at any point, and the story must survive being encountered out of order. That constraint drives an enormous amount of technical and narrative machinery.
nodes.l3: Streaming architectures, level-of-detail systems and world-partitioning techniques are documented in engine documentation and developer conference talks.
nodes.ev: Engine documentation; developer conference talks; postmortems

nodes.l1: Images computed by simulating how light actually behaves.
nodes.l2: Physically based rendering models light transport — energy conservation, real material response, actual light paths — rather than approximating an appearance. Doing that within a real-time frame budget required dedicated hardware, and the gap between offline film rendering and real-time rendering has narrowed dramatically as a result.
nodes.l3: The rendering equation was formulated in published research in 1986, and path-tracing and physically based material models are extensively documented. Hardware ray-tracing capability is documented in GPU specifications.
nodes.ev: Rendering equation literature; PBR material research; GPU specifications

nodes.l1: Modelling a system too complex to solve with an equation.
nodes.l2: Simulation is a third mode of investigation alongside theory and experiment: when a system cannot be solved analytically and cannot be experimented on, you can compute its behaviour step by step. Climate, galaxies, protein folding and epidemics are all studied this way — as are game worlds, at far lower fidelity.
nodes.l3: Monte Carlo methods date to 1940s computing work and are documented in the research literature. Scientific simulation codes and their validation studies are published, and validation against observation is the standard check.
nodes.ev: Monte Carlo literature; published simulation codes; validation studies
nodes.caution: A simulation is only as good as its assumptions. Agreement with reality must be demonstrated, never assumed.

nodes.l1: Characters with routines, goals and reactions of their own.
nodes.l2: Game AI is optimised for being interesting rather than for being intelligent. A character that plays optimally is usually no fun, so systems are designed to be readable — the player must be able to infer what the character is doing and why. Much game AI is deliberately handicapped for exactly this reason.
nodes.l3: Behaviour trees, goal-oriented action planning and utility systems are documented in technical talks and published game AI literature, including candid accounts of where the illusion breaks.
nodes.ev: Game AI literature; developer technical talks; behaviour system documentation
nodes.caution: Game AI is generally not machine learning, and it is designed to be beatable. Legibility beats optimality.

nodes.l1: Games that borrow the language of film without stopping being games.
nodes.l2: There is a real tension here. Cinema controls what you see; games hand that control to the player. Cinematic games negotiate between the two, and the long-running argument about cutscenes is a genuine design disagreement about whether authored moments are worth the cost of taking the controller away.
nodes.l3: Production documentation, virtual cinematography techniques and developer talks describe the methods. Comparative analyses of authored versus emergent moments are a standing topic in game criticism.
nodes.ev: Production documentation; virtual cinematography research; developer talks

nodes.l1: Hundreds of specialists, several years, and budgets comparable to films.
nodes.l2: A large modern game is an industrial production: artists, engineers, designers, writers, actors, audio teams, QA, localisation and production management, coordinated across studios and time zones. The scale brings capability and also risk — budgets that require enormous sales, and a well-documented pattern of excessive overtime.
nodes.l3: Credits lists, published budget figures, studio headcounts and industry labour reporting document both the scale and the working conditions, including sustained reporting on crunch.
nodes.ev: Game credits and headcounts; published budgets; labour reporting
nodes.caution: Extended crunch is a documented and recurring feature of large game production, with real costs to the people involved.

nodes.l1: A world that keeps running whether or not you are looking at it.
nodes.l2: The hard part is not size but persistence: state that survives, systems that continue off-screen, consequences that outlast the moment. Doing it fully is computationally impossible, so every open world is an elaborate arrangement of things that only exist while observed — an engineering trick that the player must never notice.
nodes.l3: Streaming, level-of-detail and simulation-culling architectures are documented in engine documentation and developer talks, which describe explicitly what is suspended when nobody is watching.
nodes.ev: Engine architecture documentation; developer technical talks

nodes.l1: Coordinating thousands of people across years and continents.
nodes.l2: At this scale the bottleneck stops being any technology and becomes coordination itself: asset pipelines, version control across terabytes, build systems, review processes, and the organisational design to keep several hundred people from blocking each other. It is much closer to shipbuilding than to writing software alone.
nodes.l3: Studio structures, pipeline tooling and production methods are documented in developer talks and postmortems. Employment figures and industry revenue data give the scale.
nodes.ev: Studio pipeline documentation; postmortems; industry employment data

nodes.l1: A series that made the open city the point rather than the setting.
nodes.l2: The series' contribution was treating the environment as the main attraction — a city dense and reactive enough to be worth existing in without a task. That reframing pushed the whole industry toward systemic worlds, and it came with sustained public controversy about content that is part of the record rather than a footnote to it.
nodes.l3: Release history, technical postmortems, sales figures and the documented regulatory and public reaction across multiple countries constitute the record.
nodes.ev: Release and sales records; technical postmortems; regulatory record
nodes.caution: The series has been the subject of long-running debate over violent content. Research on media effects is contested and does not support simple causal claims in either direction.

nodes.l1: An unreleased game, standing here for whatever the current edge happens to be.
nodes.l2: Pick any endpoint you like — this one is a placeholder for the frontier. What matters is the shape of the thing behind it: a modern game of this kind depends on semiconductor fabrication, real-time rendering research, animation principles from hand-drawn film, physics approximation, network infrastructure, thousands of people and roughly three million years of accumulated technique. No single invention is doing the work.
nodes.l3: Rockstar Games announced on its official newswire that the release moved to 19 November 2026, after an earlier date of 26 May 2026, and Take-Two reiterated the 19 November date in its fiscal first-quarter 2027 results on 7 August 2026. As of the last check of this database — 11 September 2026 — the game is unreleased, so nothing here is a claim about the finished product.
nodes.ev: Publisher and company announcements (primary sources)
nodes.caution: Unreleased at the time of writing. Release dates have moved more than once; treat any schedule as provisional.

nodes.l1: A persistent place, shared with other people, that exists only as computation.
nodes.l2: When a simulated space is persistent and shared, things start happening in it that nobody designed: economies, governance disputes, property, status, conflict, and real relationships. Virtual worlds have repeatedly become laboratories for social questions, generally by accident and usually to their operators' surprise.
nodes.l3: Long-running virtual worlds have been studied by economists, sociologists and legal scholars, with published work on in-world economies, governance and the disease-spread event in one game that epidemiologists analysed as a behavioural model.
nodes.ev: Academic studies of virtual economies and governance; platform data

nodes.l1: Organised sound, made on purpose, for no practical reason at all.
nodes.l2: Music has no obvious survival function and every known society has it. It synchronises groups, encodes memory — sung information survives far better than spoken — and moves people emotionally in ways that are cross-cultural in some respects and completely learned in others. Nobody has a settled explanation for why it exists.
nodes.l3: Bone and ivory flutes from caves in the Swabian Jura in Germany are the oldest musical instruments yet found — among them a five-hole flute made of bird bone from Hohle Fels. The excavators date them to more than 35,000 years ago, and UNESCO's World Heritage listing places the region's Ice Age finds between about 43,000 and 33,000 years ago. Replicas have been made and played, so the tuning can be checked rather than assumed.
nodes.ev: Palaeolithic bone flutes; playable replicas
nodes.caution: Why music exists is genuinely unresolved. Adaptive, by-product and cultural explanations all have serious advocates.

nodes.l1: A liquid cooled so fast its atoms never got around to forming crystals.
nodes.l2: Glass is transparent, chemically inert and shapeable when hot — a combination nothing else offered for millennia. It gave containers you can see into, windows, and eventually lenses. It is not an exaggeration to say that the microscope, the telescope, spectacles and the laboratory flask all wait on glass.
nodes.l3: Glass vessels, ingots and workshop waste survive from Bronze Age Egypt and Mesopotamia onward. Compositional analysis identifies production centres and traces trade in raw glass.
nodes.ev: Glass workshop remains; compositional sourcing; surviving vessels

nodes.l1: Plant fibre beaten to pulp and dried flat. Cheap enough to waste.
nodes.l2: The point of paper is cost. Papyrus needed a specific plant; parchment needed a herd of animals per book. Paper can be made from rags and plant waste anywhere, which drops the price of a written surface by orders of magnitude — and the price of the surface is what determines whether ordinary people can write at all.
nodes.l3: Chinese papermaking is documented in court records from the second century CE, and the technology's westward spread through Central Asia and the Islamic world into Europe is traceable through surviving documents and mill records.
nodes.ev: Early Chinese records; surviving documents; papermaking mill records

nodes.date: Woodblock ≈ 700 CE; movable type ≈ 1040 and 1450 CE
nodes.l1: Making many identical copies without copying by hand.
nodes.l2: Hand copying introduces errors and every copy costs as much as the last. Printing makes copies nearly free after setup and — the underrated part — identical, so scholars in different cities could argue over the same page and cite the same line. Reproducible reference is what made a scientific community possible across distance.
nodes.l3: Bi Sheng's ceramic movable type is described in an eleventh-century Chinese account; Korean metal type predates Gutenberg. Surviving incunabula, printers' records and the collapse in book prices document the European transition.
nodes.ev: Surviving early printed books; printers' records; book price series
nodes.caution: Movable type was invented in China and Korea well before Gutenberg. His contribution was a practical metal-type system suited to alphabetic script.

nodes.l1: A thing everyone accepts, so nobody has to want what you have.
nodes.l2: Money solves the coordination problem of barter, but the historical record suggests it did not start as barter's replacement. Credit and accounted debt appear in Mesopotamian records long before coined money, which implies money began as a unit for reckoning obligation and only later became a physical token.
nodes.l3: Cuneiform debt records substantially predate the earliest Lydian coinage of around 600 BCE. Both survive: the tablets and the coins, with several millennia between them.
nodes.ev: Cuneiform debt records; early coinage; hoard finds
nodes.caution: The textbook story that money replaced barter is not well supported. Credit systems appear first in the written record.

nodes.l1: A magnetised needle that finds north with no sky visible.
nodes.l2: Before the compass, open-water navigation depended on seeing the sun or stars — so overcast weather meant stopping. A direction reference that works in fog and at night extended the sailing season and the viable route, which is a precondition for sustained long-distance ocean voyaging.
nodes.l3: Chinese and European sources both describe mariners finding direction with a floating lodestone or a magnetised needle in the twelfth century, apparently independently. Surviving instruments and navigational treatises document how the device was refined over the following centuries.
nodes.ev: Chinese and European texts; surviving instruments; navigational treatises

nodes.l1: A machine that divides time into equal, countable pieces.
nodes.l2: Before clocks, time was local and elastic — an hour in winter was shorter than one in summer in some systems. Mechanical time is uniform and abstract, and once it exists it can be used to schedule, to pay by the hour and to measure. It is also the instrument that made precise physics and, eventually, longitude possible.
nodes.l3: Surviving tower clocks and escapement mechanisms, Huygens's 1656 pendulum work, and Harrison's marine chronometers are preserved and documented, with measured accuracy figures for each.
nodes.ev: Surviving clocks and escapements; Huygens's work; marine chronometers

nodes.l1: Shaped glass that bends light to a focus.
nodes.l2: The lens is the single component behind both the microscope and the telescope, which between them opened the very small and the very distant within a few decades of each other. Spectacles came first and are their own quiet revolution: they roughly doubled the working life of anyone whose job needed close vision.
nodes.l3: Surviving spectacle lenses, grinding equipment and the optical treatises describing focal geometry document the craft. Early instrument lenses have been measured and their performance characterised.
nodes.ev: Surviving lenses and grinding equipment; optical treatises

nodes.l1: A mixture that carries its own oxygen and therefore burns extremely fast.
nodes.l2: Gunpowder was found by Chinese alchemists looking for an elixir of immortality, which is a good reminder that research programmes rarely produce what they set out to. Its effect on fortification, state power and the balance between defence and attack was profound, and largely destructive.
nodes.l3: Chinese alchemical and military texts describe formulations from the ninth and tenth centuries onward. Surviving weapons, fortification changes and the archaeology of siege sites document the consequences.
nodes.ev: Chinese alchemical and military manuals; weapon finds; siege archaeology
nodes.caution: Included because it shaped states, cities and technology. Its primary historical use was killing people.

nodes.l1: Teaching the immune system to recognise a threat before it arrives.
nodes.l2: Vaccination is among the highest-return interventions ever devised, and smallpox — a disease that killed hundreds of millions — is the only human disease deliberately eradicated. It also produces the paradox that its own success makes it look unnecessary, which is a recurring problem for preventive measures generally.
nodes.l3: Variolation is documented in Asia and Africa before Jenner. The eradication of smallpox is documented by the World Health Organization, and long-run mortality series show the effect of each vaccination programme directly.
nodes.ev: Historical inoculation records; eradication documentation; mortality series

nodes.l1: Chemicals that kill bacteria without killing you.
nodes.l2: Before antibiotics, a scratch could be fatal and most surgery carried a serious infection risk. Their arrival changed medicine so completely that the pre-antibiotic world is hard to imagine. Resistance was predicted by Fleming himself in his Nobel lecture, and it is now a serious and growing problem.
nodes.l3: Fleming's 1928 observation, the Oxford team's clinical development in the 1940s, and subsequent resistance surveillance are all documented. Resistance rates are tracked by national and international monitoring programmes.
nodes.ev: Original research records; clinical trial history; resistance surveillance
nodes.caution: Antibiotic resistance is rising and was anticipated from the beginning. This is a gain that is not guaranteed to persist.

nodes.l1: Long molecular chains that can be shaped into almost anything.
nodes.l2: Plastics can be made light, strong, flexible, insulating, transparent or sterile as required, and cheaply. They made modern medicine, electronics and food safety possible in their present form. The same durability that makes them useful means they persist in the environment for a very long time, and that consequence took decades to register.
nodes.l3: Bakelite's 1907 synthesis and subsequent polymer chemistry are documented in patents and the research literature. Production statistics and environmental monitoring — including microplastic distribution studies — document the scale.
nodes.ev: Polymer patents and literature; production statistics; environmental monitoring
nodes.caution: Plastics' durability is both their advantage and their environmental problem. Both belong in any honest account.

nodes.l1: Sand, purified to roughly one impure atom in a billion.
nodes.l2: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust and utterly useless for electronics in its natural state. What made the semiconductor industry possible was purification and crystal growth — producing single crystals of a perfection unmatched by any other bulk manufactured material. The scarcity was never the element; it was the process.
nodes.l3: The Czochralski crystal-growth process, zone refining and semiconductor-grade purity specifications are documented in the materials science literature and in industrial standards.
nodes.ev: Crystal growth literature; purity specifications; industry standards

nodes.l1: Finding things by bouncing radio waves off them and timing the echo.
nodes.l2: Radar gave sight through darkness, cloud and distance. Its development drove microwave electronics hard — the cavity magnetron in particular — and that wartime push fed directly into post-war electronics, radio astronomy and, eventually, the microwave oven, which is a rather blunt illustration of dual-use technology.
nodes.l3: Development records, surviving equipment and IEEE milestone documentation record the systems and their performance. The technology transfer into civilian electronics is well traced.
nodes.ev: Development records; surviving equipment; IEEE milestones

nodes.l1: A machine placed in orbit, falling around the Earth indefinitely.
nodes.l2: Orbit gives a vantage point over a whole hemisphere at once, which is why satellites transformed communication, weather forecasting, navigation, mapping and climate monitoring simultaneously. Most of what is known about global climate change comes from instruments that had to be put above the atmosphere to work.
nodes.l3: Launch records, orbital catalogues and the continuous data archives from Earth observation missions are public. Satellite counts and launch-cost series are tracked over decades.
nodes.ev: Launch and orbital records; Earth observation data archives

nodes.l1: Knowing exactly where you are, anywhere, from timing signals in space.
nodes.l2: Position is computed from the tiny differences in arrival time of signals from several satellites — which means the system depends on clocks accurate to nanoseconds, and on correcting for relativistic time dilation. Without applying both special and general relativity, positions would drift by kilometres per day. It is the most routine practical use of Einstein's physics there is.
nodes.l3: System specifications, published accuracy analyses and the documented relativistic corrections are public. Independent verification of the relativistic effects is a standard textbook case.
nodes.ev: System specifications; accuracy analyses; relativistic correction documentation

nodes.date: ≈ 5,000 years ago onward, earliest in Egypt and Mesopotamia
nodes.l1: A unit of weight that means the same thing in every market.
nodes.l2: Trade beyond a small circle of trust needs a shared standard, not just mutual goodwill — a trader from one city has to be able to check a merchant's weights against a known reference. States backed this with enforcement: inspected weight sets, stamped denominations, and penalties for short-weighting. Once weight and length are standardized, price comparison, taxation and large contracts between strangers all become practical.
nodes.l3: Sets of stone and bronze weights, calibrated against each other and often stamped with a denomination, survive by the thousands from Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley and the Aegean. Comparing weight sets across sites is how archaeologists reconstruct which regions shared a trading standard.
nodes.ev: Calibrated weight sets; stamped denominations; cross-site weight comparisons

nodes.date: Temple and merchant lending ≈ 4,000 years ago onward; formal banks from medieval Italy
nodes.l1: Other people's money, held, lent and tracked by a third party.
nodes.l2: Banking separates saving from spending: a deposit can be lent to someone else while the depositor still expects it back on demand. Mesopotamian temples and merchant houses acted as lenders and safekeepers millennia before anything called a 'bank' existed; what changed in medieval Italy was formalizing the ledger, the interest calculation and the cross-city transfer into a specialised trade of its own.
nodes.l3: Cuneiform loan contracts record interest rates, collateral and repayment terms from the early second millennium BCE. Medieval Italian merchant-bank account books are the direct ancestor of the modern bank statement.
nodes.ev: Cuneiform loan contracts; medieval Italian merchant-bank ledgers

nodes.date: Formalised in print by Luca Pacioli, 1494 (Venice); practised earlier by Italian merchants
nodes.l1: Every transaction recorded twice, so the books have to balance.
nodes.l2: Double-entry turns bookkeeping into a self-checking system: each transaction is entered as a debit in one account and a matching credit in another, so total debits must equal total credits.
